blurb: Corral played for the Rebels as both a freshman and sophomore, but his career didn't take off until Lane Kiffin came to Oxford. Kiffin's offense took advantage of Corral's athleticism, rocket arm and quick release. The RPO-heavy offense attacked every level of the field, and Corral saw his grade take a massive leap. However, the offense isn't particularly translatable to the NFL, meaning Corral still comes with some question marks. He used play action on 60.4% of his dropbacks in 2021, the highest rate in the FBS.
pros: Athlete who happens to play quarterback. Mobility is a big plus. Compact motion. Generates serious torque during his throwing motion. Stands tall in the pocket and rips from a consistent base. Accurate to all levels.
cons: Slim frame. Listed at 205 pounds. Already dealt with multiple injuries in 2021. Not much throw shaping on his tape. Lasers only. Looks like a different quarterback and lacks confidence when forced past first read.
where_wins: DIST R IBU T IN G Corral is at his best when playing point guard — distributing the ball quickly and swiftly to all levels of the field. NFL OC's will take advantage of his timing and accuracy in the RPO and quick passing game.
what_role: P LA Y BOOK OP EN ER Corral has serious tools that any offensive coordinator would love to try and mold. He also needs some serious molding, though. He's a project who needs to learn behind a veteran early in his career.
what_improve: T OU CH Corral was hardly asked to run dropback passing concepts at Ole Miss. He is exceptional on simple rhythm concepts/RPOs, but when asked to expand his vision and identify where to go with the ball, his play suffers.
bottom_line: Drafting Corral should be seen as an investment, not a quick fix to a team’s passing offense.

blurb: Eleby first got starting experience as a true freshman back in 2018 when an injury to starter Jon Wassink forced him into action against Toledo late in the year. He earned a 63.7 overall grade in five games before ceding that starting job back to Wassink in 2019. Once the job was his again in 2020, Eleby was a revelation. He earned a 91.5 passing grade in six games throwing to the likes of 2021 2nd-round pick Dee Eskridge and potential 2022 1st-rounder Skyy Moore. He couldn't sustain that for a full season in 2021, however, as he started putting the ball in harm's way more. Maryland Heights, MO
pros: Works pockets confidently. Consistently climbs with eyes downfield. Can hit drive throws downfield when he steps into it. Some impressive lasers on tape. Attacking mentality while still taking care of the football. 11.0 yard ADoT in career.
cons: Erratic ball placement. Gets amplified off- platform or on the move. Short with compact frame. Not going to do him any favors. Panicky under pressure. Can visibly see everything speed up.
where_wins: NA
what_role: NA
what_improve: NA
bottom_line: Eleby may not have the ideal developmental skillset, but he has sustained performance with an NFL-caliber arm.

blurb: Howell has started from Day 1 for the Tarheels. As a freshman in 2019, he put up the second-highest graded season we've charted from a true freshman quarterback, behind only Trevor Lawrence. He built upon that with a superb sophomore campaign, where he racked up impressive throw after impressive throw. After losing his top two receivers and rushers from 2020, Howell and the Tar Heels offense took a massive step Slower back in 2021. He countered by running Russell more than ever and went for 1,106 yards on Wilson the ground. Monroe, NC
pros: Arm talent for days. Elite deep ball thrower over course of his career. Light on his feet in the pocket. Can make subtle and not so subtle moves to buy time. Thick build. Shrugs off defenders with relative ease with 65 broken tackles in 202.
cons: One and run. First instinct is to drop eyes and bolt. Inexplicably turns down open receivers too often. Not enough anticipatory throws. Offense was almost all RPOs and go-balls, leading the nation in both.
where_wins: A R M T A LEN T From his arm to his mentality, Howell is a downfield passer. He's one of the most prolific we've seen in the PFF College era (2014-present). He'll have to go to an offense that's willing to attack downfield regularly.
what_role: DOWN F IELD P A SSER No page of the playbook is off limits with Howell. He has the arm for any passing concept, can run between the tackles and also create on his own outside. While he is a project in some ways, he could still start early on.
what_improve: P R OG R ESSION S Howell can't be so reliant on scrambling at the next level — 13% of his dropbacks resulted in scrambles in 2021. He's not that kind of athlete. He has to be more patient and quicker through progressions from clean pockets.
bottom_line: Howell has his areas for growth, but his sheer physical tools are undeniable. He has more to offer than what was showcased in the Tar heel's offense.

blurb: Pickett has been on the NFL's radar for quite some time. He took over as the starter as a sophomore in 2018 and would undoubtedly have been drafted had he come out in 2019 after earning a 75.0 overall grade. It just would have been somewhere on Day 3. That's where his draft stock lay dormant until this past season when Pickett took an unprecedented leap in year four as a starter. He saw his big-time throw rate nearly double from 2020 and his turnover-worthy play rate hit a career low. Oakhurst, NJ
pros: Accuracy on the move is a big plus. Pinpoint outside the pocket. Can sting a far hash out route with ease. Obvious arm talent from pocket and on move. Mobile but always has his eyes downfield. Terrific at creating space to work.
cons: Holds the ball until the bitter end. Second- highest time to throw in the country. Bad habit of throwing off back foot. Worrisome how often he does so on vertical shots. One-year wonder. One of the biggest single- season grading leaps we've seen in Year 5.
where_wins: QB F EEL Pickett has a natural feel that's uncoachable in a lot of ways. Whether it's throwing guys open, understanding receiver leverage, avoiding the rush or keying blitzes, Pickett gets a lot of the little things already.
what_role: A LL- A R OU N D QB Between his combination of experience and NFL-translateable skills, Pickett is as ready as any quarterback in the draft class to start out the gate. The question is: How high is his ceiling?
what_improve: P R OCESSIN G SP EED He has to speed up his process in the league. He'll work through reads under the assumption he can always buy himself more time. "Ball out" has to be his first thought at the next level instead of "break pocket."
bottom_line: Pickett has enough lingering questions to scare teams off, but his 2021 tape didn't have a ton of holes.

blurb: Purdy was a revelation as a true freshman in 2018. He took over as the full-time starter in Week 6 of that season and finished with an 89.3 overall grade in nine games with only one of those against a non-power-5 opponent (and it was his lowest-graded game that year). That year, though, he had Hakeem Butler hauling in his deep balls. Ever since, he's struggled mightily to produce down the football field and it's been reflected in his plateaued grades. He went from an 8.3% big-time throw rate as a freshman to 4.2% as a sophomore, to 3.4% as a junior, and finally 2.4% as a senior. Gilbert, AZ
pros: Agile and aware in the pocket. Extremely low 12.9% career sack conversion rate. Plus accuracy. Highest on-target rate of any QB in the draft class last year. Quick, tight release that can get the job done on the move as well.
cons: Arm strength is borderline by NFL standards. Already limited downfield in college. Field vision narrows far too often. Tunnel in on his guys and slow to come off. Plays tight. Few calculated risks. Will speed up internal clock and check down too often.
where_wins: NA
what_role: NA
what_improve: NA
bottom_line: Purdy won't look too out of place in an NFL offense, but he also won't elevate above if thrown into a bad situation.

blurb: Ridder is now synonymous with the rise of Cincinnati football as he's been at Cincinnati all five years of the Fickell era, starting the last four. He had a Jalen Hurts- esque career progression from true freshman to senior year, as he went from a player who looked undraftable early on to one who consistently won from the pocket later in his career. He's done a tremendous job of improving upon his weaknesses every single year, and you see that in his grade Louisville, KY
pros: Quick processor. Best in the class. Already plays at NFL speed mentally. Straight-line gas in the open field. Big-play threat as a runner if unaccounted for. Coaches rave about his work ethic and leadership. Has improved weaknesses every year.
cons: Slightly elongated throwing motion. Little dip in his cocking phase. Thin frame. Not as elusive as other, which has led to high sack conversion rates. Beat up bad competition. 70.6 passing grade against Power-5 schools last two years.
where_wins: P R OCESSIN G SP EED Ridder is a decisive and quick pocket-passer who has good enough arm talent to hit defenses over the top. While he's not much of a runner himself, his speed demands that he's accounted for.
what_role: QU ICK P A SSER Ridder isn't scheme limited by any means. He can step in Day1 and not look out of place as a starter. Utilizing his legs as a weapon is a plus but isn't necessary for him to succeed at the next level.
what_improve: BA LL P LA CEMEN T Ridder's ball placement is still below-average by NFL standards, and it often is even worse early in games. He's too refined technically for this to dramatically change.
bottom_line: Ridder is the most NFL-ready quarterback in the class and still has areas for growth. In a class full of developmental QBs, he has the work ethic to bet on.

blurb: Strong dealt with degenerative knee issues coming out of high school, which limited his college offers to lower-tier programs despite upper-tier talent. At Nevada, he was starting by the time he was a redshirt freshman in 2019. Since then, he's blossomed into one of the most prolific passers in college football. Nevada put it all on his right arm in 2021, as he dropped back to pass nearly 50 times a game on Ryan Mal l ett average. His calling card is his ability to Wi th Touch drive the ball outside the numbers, and he earned a 91.1 passing grade on such throws last year. Vacaville, CA
pros: Gorgeous tight spiral paired with quick release. Ideal combo for NFL windows. Arm talent opens entire field. Five 50-plus-yard completions — most in FBS. Offense was entirely on his right arm. 50+ dropbacks in six straight games.
cons: Serious knee problems (Osteochondritis dissecans). Possibly career threatening. Statue. No escapability. Has broken just six total tackles in career. Pocket drifter. Too quick to eliminate options while drifting from non-existent pressure.
where_wins: OU T SIDE T H E N U MBER S Strong has the coveted ability to consistently attack outside the numbers. His 91.5 passing grade on such throws is the highest among the top quarterbacks in the class. That only grows in value in the NFL.
what_role: P OCKER P A SSER Strong is a project pocket-passer who needs to go to a downfield passing offense. He has all the arm talent a team could want, but with little more in the way of polish for the position, he's likely a backup out the gate.
what_improve: P OCKET MOV EMEN T To win solely from the pocket in the NFL, a QB has to be better at manipulating pockets than Strong. He needs to master subtle movements with his body and eyes to better avoid pressure and create throwing lanes.
bottom_line: Strong's knee issues will have him off some boards, but his play style should limit much of its effect. He's an intriguing arm talent project.

blurb: In his sophomore season, Willis went toe- to-toe with then-freshman Bo Nix for the starting quarterback position at Auburn back in 2019. Nix obviously won out, but Willis is getting the last laugh. He transferred to Liberty that fall and has been their starter the past two seasons. The Flames quarterback stuffed the stat sheets not only as a passer but as a runner, too. This past season, he broke more tackles (89) than any player on the ground, including running backs. He also put up the third-highest big- time throw rate we've charted in a single season (11.0%). Atlanta, GA
pros: Arguably the strongest arm in the draft. Can get velocity from any body position. Adds massive value as runner. Draftable RB if he switched — 146 career broken tackles. Footwork improved a ton from 2020 to 2021. Has shown he can take coaching.
cons: Base is woefully inconsistent. Has made strides, but it still shows up too often. Eyes telegraph his throws regularly. Will stare daggers through his targets. Level of competition was poor. Had some ugly outings against Power-5 defenses.
where_wins: T OOLS Willis wins when playing schoolyard ball. His creativity on the move as both a thrower and runner is special. He can provide instant offense at any level of football.
what_role: A T H LET E Willis isn't a Day-1 starter and needs to go to an offense built around his legs. Parking him behind an established quarterback in that mold to get acclimated to the NFL game would be his best bet.
what_improve: P OCKET P R ESEN CE Willis' pocket presence is still an issue. Slight pressure causes him to fully break out of play structure. Playing quicker and more on schedule have to be a point of emphasis.
bottom_line: Willis is a pure project due to all the tools in the world to work with. Developing him behind an established mobile quarterback would be ideal.

blurb: Zappe set records for three years at Houston Baptist before heading to Western Kentucky to set even more. He set single- season FBS marks for passing yards (5,967) and passing touchdowns (62) in his lone year with the Hilltoppers. While the numbers are gaudy, the situation was also set up for success. He was under pressure at the lowest rate of any quarterback in college football last season (12.9% of dropbacks). Victoria, TX
pros: Creativity with his ball placement. Understands leverage and throws receivers open. Quick to scan. Often works back to opposite side of field while staying in rhythm. Handled insane volume with 730 dropbacks last year. Broke FBS yards and TD records
cons: Below-average arm by NFL standards. Had a Hail-Mary from midfield come up short. Footwork suffers mightily when forced to move in pocket. Falls off a lot of throws. Had all day to work with massive pockets. Was pressured on only 12.5% of dropbacks.
where_wins: G A MER Zappe is a gamer. He finds ways to get the job done and had a high command of the Hilltoppers offense. He'll have to dominate the quick game at the next level.
what_role: H IG H - EN D BA CKU P Zappe isn't a toolsy prospect. He's a glue guy backup who could develop into a starter. Competent backup play on a cheap rookie deal can still provide good value in the NFL.
what_improve: P LA Y U N DER P R ESSU R E Zappe has to come up with better answers under pressure. The pockets he's going to work from in the NFL are tight, and his ability to handle those has to improve.
bottom_line: While he may not blow anyone away physically, Zappe won't look out of place on an NFL field. He figures to be at least a backup for a long time.

blurb: Allgeier may look like a bruiser, but he's a little niftier than that moniker implies. To break tackles at the rate he has the past two seasons — even if the competition wasn't the greatest — one has to be. Despite having that elusiveness, Allgeier still knows who he is. He will rarely stop his feet behind the line of scrimmage or go searching for home runs. While he has the profile of a volume back, Allgeier still needs to clean up the fumbles after fumbling six times at BYU. Fontana, CA
pros: No nonsense running style that's perfect for a bigger back. Vision is a plus. Always seems to be gaining ground toward the open hole. Outstanding pass-blocker. Finds work and eliminates threats.
cons: Acceleration is lacking. Needs a runway to get a head of steam. Runs like a power back, but at only 220- pounds, he wouldn't qualify as one in the NFL Ran behind an insanely dominant BYU offensive line over the past two seasons.
where_wins: N O- N ON SEN SE R U N N IN G Allgeier wins by consistently maximizing his run blocking. He's not going to pass up open holes searching for big plays. He'll get you what's blocked and a little extra.
what_role: Z ON E- SCH EME R B Allgeier would be perfect in a zone-heavy scheme to take advantage of his one-cut running style and vision. While he's not limited per se, that's easily his cleanest projection.
what_improve: CR EA T IV IT Y Allgeier could stand to be more creative when he gets into the open field. He maintains his no nonsense running style in the open field and often seeks out contact instead of avoiding it.
bottom_line: There isn't much about Allgeier that makes you say 'wow,' but there's also not much to dislike, either.

blurb: Badie spent three years toiling as the receiving back to now Charger Larry Rountree's bell-cow workload on the ground. Once he got that bell-cow workload this past season, Badie took his game to another level. He was not only electric on the ground but also reliable through the air. Despite not looking the part of an every down back, he finished second in the FBS with 323 touches last season. Memphis, TN
pros: Burst and size to fit through the tightest of creases at the line. Proficient receiver out of the backfield for three straight seasons. Small, but doesn't run like it. Wiling to pick up the tough yards when he has to.
cons: Well below size you'd like for an every down back with little room to add more mass. Tough runner, but a lot of his broken tackles are unlikely to translate to the NFL. All too often a speedbump in pass protection. Not sure that improves
where_wins: BU R ST Badie's ability to get up to full speed from a standstill is why he'll find a role at the next level. Everyone is looking to get his kind of suddenness on the field regardless of position.
what_role: SCA T BA CK Badie is going to be the passing game back in whatever system he goes to. Don't expect for him to get more than a few carries a game at the next level.
what_improve: P A SS P R OT ECT ION Badie has to attack better in pass protection if he wants to see the field. At his size, he can't afford to sit and wait for NFL linebackers or he'll get bowled over.
bottom_line: Badie is in that physical limbo where he's too small for OC's to trust every down and not athletic enough to justify his deficiencies.

blurb: Chandler spent his first four seasons at Tennessee in a time share role every single year. Despite seeing the bulk of the carries his last few years there, Chandler grad transferred to North Carolina this past fall to see an expanded role. He set career highs in every category imaginable for the Tarheels. Known for his speed, Chandler more than doubled his previous career high for explosive runs. Nashville, TN
pros: Blazer in the open field. Over 10% of his carries in 2021 went for 15+ yards. Quicks that strike fear in linebackers when releasing on routes out of the backfield. Extensive pass game experience. 91 targets in his career.
cons: Undersized for the position and doesn't run with desired physicality to counteract it. Middling elusiveness. Doesn't have that kind of shake in the open field. Very old for a running back prospect. Turns 24 in May.
where_wins: NA
what_role: NA
what_improve: NA
bottom_line: If you want speed, Chandler has it. That's the extent of his skillset that NFL teams will value

blurb: You may have heard that James is the younger brother of Vikings back Dalvin Cook. Even if you haven't, you’d realize right away by his running style. The two have the same distinct sharp cuts in their running style and near instantaneous acceleration. The only difference being the 3-4 older brother has around 10-15 pounds on the younger. That was a big deal at Georgia and why he never had more than 12 carries in a single game. Even if he’s not a bell-cow in the NFL, you’ll want him in your backfield for his explosiveness in the passing Miami, FL
pros: Lightning rod. Can blaze past linebackers. struggles to churn. Reaches top speed in a hurry and doesn't seem to lose any when he cuts. Very natural receiver. One drop on 68 career catchable passes.
cons: Built like a wide receiver. Light lower half that Not much wiggle to his game despite being undersized. Still a cut-and-go runner. Scat back. Georgia specifically made sure he didn't have to pass protect..
where_wins: H OME- R U N S Cook is a mismatch in the passing game because he's far too nimble even for NFL linebackers. Anytime Georgia schemed up on-one-one's for Cook, they were throwing his way.
what_role: SCA T BA CK Cook is the change-of-pace back who teams can get creative with. He can split wide and run routes or get vertical from the backfield.
what_improve: MU SCLE MA SS Obviously, if he wants to be anything more than a receiving back at the next level, he has to put on muscle. Can't be a three-down back at his size.
bottom_line: Cook is like a mini-version of his brother Dalvin. He's a big play waiting to happen when he gets the ball in space.

blurb: Ealy came to Ole Miss as both a highly touted running back and outfielder. He played both football and baseball as a freshman before COVID hit and has been focusing on football since. Ealy immediately saw action as a change of pace back his first year with the Rebels. His role has really never evolved since and at his size is unlikely to in the NFL. Ealy can still make an impact as a change of pace back in an offense willing to be creative with him. Flowood, MS
pros: As good a contact balance as you'll see from a small back. Human pinball.. Such subtle body control and balance. Like he knows what the defenders going to do. Tough as nails for a back his size. Take a lick and keeps chugging.
cons: Too comfortable stalling his feet in the backfield. Can't get away with that in the NFL. Scat back only. Cannot hold up in pass protection at his size. Not comfortable operating in tight quarters. Needed the space Ole Miss provided.
where_wins: NA
what_role: NA
what_improve: NA
bottom_line: If he were 20-pounds heavier, we'd be talking about the best running back in the class. Even still, he can offer something as a change of pace back.

blurb: Ford started his career off at Alabama and struggled to even see the football field behind the likes of Najee Harris and Brian Robinson. After two seasons there, he transferred to Cincinnati. In 2020, he was the dash to Gerrid Doaks' smash in a time-share. In 2021, Ford took over as the lead dog and flourished. The worry was his boom-or-bust nature with four games this past season where he averaged under 4.0 yards per Tampa, FL
pros: Explosive out of his cuts with speed to run away from linebackers with ease. Consistent hands on tape. Didn't have a drop on 31 catches in his career. Nose for the end zone. 30 of his 318 career carries ended in scores.
cons: Slightly built and runs high. Limits his pop on contact. Six fumbles on 311 carries the last three years. Loses confidence when reads aren't clean and will patter into the line.
where_wins: N A T U R A L A T H LET ICISM Ford's a very easy mover in space. He's not limited in any way, shape or form by his athletic ability at the next level.
what_role: P R OJECT R B Ford is more athlete than running back still. He's one heck of an athlete but is very rough around the edges in things he'll have to do in the NFL.
what_improve: BA LL SECU R IT Y No one is going to let him see the field in the NFL with the kind of ball security issues he showed in college. He'd lead the league in fumbles with a full workload at that rate.
bottom_line: Ford has NFL-caliber athleticism, but he's not NFL-ready to carry a large workload on tape.

blurb: With the bell-cow type growing out of vogue more so every year in the college game, Hall was a true throwback. His carries in the past two seasons were more than any other Power Five running back in the country. His 41 scores were also five more than any back in college football. Iowa State ran their offense through him largely because there are very few weaknesses to his game. Whatever concept or play you want to draw up, chances are Hall can execute. Wichita, KS
pros: As a receiver, he's been one of the most difficult running backs to bring down in the country. Balance is tremendous. Can get in and out of awkward body positions. Accustomed to running behind less than stellar run blocking at Iowa State.
cons: Lacks the ideal burst out of his cuts that you'd want in the NFL. Worried a little about his tackle-breaking numbers translating at his height. Can run high between the tackles. Not going to drive through a defensive lineman.
where_wins: CON T A CT BA LA N CE Hall wins with his absolute refusal to go down. He doesn't give up on runs and will churn his legs to the bitter end. More often than not, it takes multiple guys to bring him down.
what_role: BELL COW Hall can quite obviously fill the bell-cow role in an offense: He's touched the ball more than any running back in the country the past two seasons (590 times).
what_improve: LOWER IN G SH OU LDER Hall can stand to put his foot in the ground and drive into contact a touch more in situations where there's not much available. He has power back traits but would be well served to add the power back bulk.
bottom_line: Hall has a well-rounded skill set that can elevate him to RB1, but there's some questions about the translatability of his game.

blurb: Knight has one of the wildest statistical profiles of any player in the draft class. He starter in a time share as a true freshman gaining 745 yards on 136 carries at 5.5 yards per. Over the next two seasons, he's had nearly identical attempts and yardage figures with only his scoring fluctuating in any meaningful way. I'd say he could have upped his draft stock by returning to school, but we'd likely see more of the same. Bailey, NC
pros: Slippery lower half with tremendous body control in his cuts. Feet and body control a point guard in basketball. Productive at a very young age. Only turned 21 in April.
cons: Crippling inconsistent vision. Needs to see the whole runway before he's ready to launch. Serious fumble problems. Seven on 419 career carries. Flashed some rough hands early in his career. Six drops on 53 career catchable
where_wins: NA
what_role: NA
what_improve: NA
bottom_line: Knight is still young and ascending, but his game is so rough around the edges that he'll struggle to see a field early in his career.

blurb: "Why? Because I'm a Gator, bro." That was Dameon Pierce's answer to why he was playing in Florida's bowl game, even though he'd already solidified his draft stock. That also perfectly describes Pierce's game. He's willing to do the dirty work without any sort of accolade. Pierce is one of the best and 3-4 most willing pass-protectors in the draft class. He can seamlessly fill in as a third- down back in the league from Day 1. Even Slimmer if he's never been a bell-cow at the NFL C.J. level, Pierce has that kind of size and ability. Anderson Bainbridge, GA
pros: At 215 pounds of almost pure muscle, he's built like an armored vehicle. His low center of gravity allows him to stop and cut on dimes. Tough stiff arm. Consistently shrugs off first man. than 106 carries in a season.
cons: Middling burst and long speed. Not much of a home-run hitter. Gets too greedy with his cuts at times and slipped on a handful of runs last year. Why wasn't he featured more? Never had more
where_wins: ST R EN G T H Pierce wins by consistently grinding out tough yards. He runs with great pad-level, and it's rare to see him stuck in his tracks on contact.
what_role: T IME SH A R E R B Pierce isn't a limited player by any means, but given his history at Florida, he's likely best suited for a time-share situation in the NFL.
what_improve: WOR KLOA D Pierce needs to prove that he can handle a larger workload. Not only did he not receive a lot of carries at Florida, but he never played more than 23 snaps in any single game.
bottom_line: Just because Pierce split time at Florida doesn't mean he's not a bell-cow candidate in the NFL. He's a consistent tackle breaker with real deal juice.

blurb: It's a shame that Robinson was stuck behind a first-rounder in his same recruiting class because he would have been in the NFL a long time ago had he not been. He's earned well-above-average rushing grades ever since his true freshman year but shined this past season as a bell-cow. Robinson is the kind of back that seems to gain more steam the more times he touches the ball. He may not be given that opportunity at the next level, but he will almost assuredly shine in short-yardage situations. Tuscaloosa, AL
pros: Runs behind pads and wants to deliver the blow. Great short-yardage back. Knows who he is and his limitations. Won't see him pitter pattering behind the line. Not a ton of tread on the tires despite his age with 545 carries in five seasons.
cons: Not a big-play threat or home-run hitter by any means. Won't have physical advantage in the NFL and is high cut for a pure power back. Surprisingly rough around the edges in pass protection. Lacks aggression there.
where_wins: P H Y SICA LIT Y Robinson wins with physicality. He's bigger and stronger than you, and he knows it. His violent running style will serve him well in the NFL.
what_role: SH OR T Y A R DA G E R B This is a short-yardage back who can also get opposing defenses out of two-high shells. He'll give a middle finger to your light boxes like he did against Cincinnati in the College Football Playoff semifinals.
what_improve: P A SS P R O T ECH N IQU E Robinson, at least, has to work on his technique in pass protection if he wants to be anything more than an early-down back. He quite obviously has the size to do it.
bottom_line: Robinson is a two-down thumper. Bring him in for goal-line and short- yardage situations but don't expect much more.

blurb: Spiller has been the starting back for Texas A&M ever since he first stepped on campus in 2019. While his three seasons in College Station look identical from a statistical perspective, the PFF grading tells a much different story. The biggest leap came this past offseason when he trimmed down considerably and became a much more dynamic back, which showed in his broken- tackle numbers. Atlanta, GA
pros: Top notch feet for a bigger back. Jump-cut ability is a big plus. Dropped 10 pounds after his sophomore season and became a much more elusive back. Easy three-down projection. Can be a plus pass-blocker and receiver.
cons: Long speed is lacking. Linebackers can catch him from behind. Costs himself yards by dancing too much. Doesn't routinely maximize his runs. On the tall side for a back, and he gets chopped down easier than you'd like.
where_wins: V ER SA T ILIT Y Spiller wins with by being able to execute any role asked of him. Whether it's taking 30 carries in a game, seeing a half-dozen targets, or being assignment sound in pass protection, Spiller won't look out of place.
what_role: G A P - SCH EME R B Spiller has the size and pedigree to handle an every-down role. He's a better fit for a gap scheme where his overly patient running style isn't likely to be a detriment.
what_improve: DECISIV EN ESS Spiller has to be more decisive as a runner at the next level. He can get away with stopping his feet behind the line of scrimmage to find the perfect hole in college, but that won't fly in the league.
bottom_line: Spiller may not have high-end traits, but he has a complete NFL skill set.

blurb: It's been a long time coming for the redshirt senior back who's been carrying the load for the Jackrabbits ever since 2018. That season he averaged over 9.0 yards per carry and went for 1,116 yards. Since then, he's been known for his explosive ability with 76 of his 627 career attempts going for 15- plus yards. With his speed, he'll continue to be a big play threat in every offense he's in. If he can improve his hands (nine drops on 71 career catchable), he can also be a weapon in the pass game. Little Rock, AR
pros: Can get north-south in the blink of an eye. Top notch standstill burst. Good luck catching him in the open field. Top- end speed is elite. Runs square to the line as long as possible. Allows him to change lanes easily.
cons: No churn ability. Outstretched arms from defensive linemen can bring him down. Decelerates into contact too often instead of exploding through. Drop issues every single year. Nine drops on 71 career catchable.
where_wins: A CCELER A T ION Strong can get to the second-level of the defense and beyond in a flash if you're not careful. Anytime he touches the ball, opposing defenses have to be wary of the big play.
what_role: CH A N G E OF P A CE BA CK Strong isn't the bell cow prototype by any means. He's a gifted athlete that looks more like a wide receiver playing the position at times than a true running back. He'd be best in a time share with a bigger back
what_improve: H A R D- N OSED R U N N IN G Strong has to grind out tough yards better. There won't always be a crease for him to hit cleanly at the next level. When that's the case, Strong has to come into the hole with more ferocity.
bottom_line: Strong is the best home-run hitter in the class, but don't expect him to ever garner a large workload in your offense.

blurb: Despite grading out exceptionally well ever since his true freshman season, Walker wallowed in relative anonymity his first two seasons at Wake Forest before transferring to Michigan State. It was in East Lansing where he'd develop a reputation worthy of becoming a Heisman finalist. Running backs aren't supposed to carry teams in college football the way he did. He led the nation in broken tackles and tied Jonathan Taylor and Rashaad Penny for the highest yards after contact average for a running back with 250+ carries in a season (4.5). Arlington, TN
pros: So many ways to win as a runner. Power, speed, elusiveness — you name it. Explodes through small creases with no hesitation — a necessary skill in the NFL. Handled a huge workload and didn't slow down — 20+ carries in six straight games.
cons: Wants no part of pass protection. Protects like he doesn't want to get hurt. Good, not great, athlete. Lacks high-end traits that get drafted early. Very limited work in the passing game — 18 career catches.
where_wins: EV ER Y WH ER E In a word...everywhere. It's what makes him so dangerous. He can lower a shoulder one play, outrun a defender on another and shake one on the next. All-around dynamic player.
what_role: BELL COW Walker can quite clearly handle a bell-cow role. He's scheme and usage diverse. He can fill whatever role a team needs.
what_improve: P A SS P R OT ECT ION Walker has to buy in as a pass-blocker to see a bell-cow role in the NFL. Coaches at the next level won't let him see the field on passing downs with what he put on tape as a pass-blocker in 2021.
bottom_line: Walker isn't a one-year wonder. He's the real deal and has an all-around NFL skill set.

blurb: White is one of the most well-traveled prospects in the entire draft class. He started at Nebraska-Kearney before spending two years at Mt. San Antonio College. Then, in 2020, he transferred to Arizona State and could well have been NFL-ready now if not for COVID. White took obvious control of the starting running back position for the Sun Devils in 2020, as he averaged an absurd 10 yards per carry, Slower though that came in only four games and Kenyan 42 carries. He followed it up this past season Drake by proving it was no fluke with 1,000 yards and 15 scores. Kansas City, MO
pros: Easy acceleration out of his cuts. Can beat you to the edge. Shimmy shake that will snatch an opposing defender's ankles. So creative in space. Wasn't used as a returner but could have a future there.
cons: Loosey-goosey running style that is akin to a wide receiver playing running back. Not confident between the tackles. Eyes look to bounce quickly. Work in progress in pass protection. Has the desire, but not the refinement.
where_wins: SP A CE P LA Y White wins with the ball in space. The good news is it's very easy to get it to him there because he has some of the best receiving ability in the draft class.
what_role: 3 R D DOWN R B/ WR CON V ER T White is a change-of-pace or receiving back early on in his career. He may even be a sneaky candidate to switch to wide receiver full-time, but you don't see a lot of that.
what_improve: DISCIP LIN ED R U N N IN G White needs more reps with some discipline instilled into his running style. He's going to miss a lot of holes between the tackles in the league without it.
bottom_line: White is the rare project at running back. If you can reign his running style in a little, he can be a playmaker.

blurb: White was the absolute perfect back to personify the 2021 Georgia Bulldogs. By any measure an elite athlete, White runs like he's the one trying to tackle you. It was a slow build for White into that guy. A highly touted recruit, White redshirted as a freshman before seeing spot action in 2019. He's been part of a time share the last two years, but the tape and grades clearly showed a different level of physical prowess that he ran with in 2021. Laurinburg, NC
pros: Wound up 214 pounder. Explosiveness that will translate to the league. Knows where he wins. Lowers pads into contact at full force regularly. Powerful lower half that won't round cuts going north-south.
cons: Creativity is lacking. Not one to create on his own Disregarded in passing game. 16 career catches. X
where_wins: NA
what_role: NA
what_improve: NA
bottom_line: White may not go too far above and beyond what's blocked ever, but he'll put an exclamation point on every run.

blurb: White started his career off at Florida State where they moved him to the defensive side of the ball. He saw 119 snaps at linebacker his redshirt freshman year in before he was ruled academically inelligible and transferrred to Iowa Western Community College to play running back once again. After one year there he transferred to South Carolina where he barely saw the field behind Kevin Harris. Finally he got a bit of a timeshare role in 2021 where he broke tackles left and right. North Fort Myers, FL
pros: Scat back-esque precision in his cuts. Can stop on a dime and run deadly routes. Acceleration on tape that wasn't reflected in his athletic testing. Lower body flexibility that matches the elite at the position in the NFL.
cons: Hands went clang in lone season with receiving work. Four drops on 23 catchable. Haphazard running style led to very few opportunities. 105 career carries. Pass protects like a traffic cone. Does little more than stand in the defenders path.
where_wins: NA
what_role: NA
what_improve: NA
bottom_line: White is a project in every way you can think of as a running back. He's also capable of things physically no one else in the class is.

blurb: After barely playing as a true freshman in 2019, Kyren Williams has been the focal point of the offense the past two seasons. Not only in the running game but as a receiver, as well. Williams' 77 receptions the past two years were the second most on Notre Dame. He did all that despite checking in under 200 pounds. The one red flag on his production profile would be his eight fumbles over that span. Saint Louis, MO
pros: The most willing pass-blocker in the class. Sticks his nose into the fray. Extremely reliable receiver. Good hands and can run a mean angle route. Defenders don't want to see his stiff arm being thrown their way. Packs a punch.
cons: Just an OK athlete who has no real trump card trait to hang his hat on. Production decreased when his offensive line took a step backward in early 2021. On the smaller side for the position, barely scraping 200 pounds.
where_wins: P A SS G A ME Williams wins in the passing game. Whether it's his work in pass protection or his natural hands, he makes an impact on passing downs.
what_role: P A SS DOWN R B At the very worst, he is a third-down back. He can be more than that, but he's a shoe-in to add value in that regard.
what_improve: SIZ E Size is his biggest issue, but it's not like he has a ton of room on his frame to pack on mass. He may just be stuck as a time-share back and never a bell cow.
bottom_line: Great fit for teams that involve their running back a lot in the passing game.

blurb: Austin started out on the Memphis track team while also participating as a walk-on for the football team. After a slow start, Austin finally broke out as the Tigers leading receiver as a redshirt junior in 2020. He showed the ability to take it to the house from anywhere on the football field with 11 scores that season. Almost counterintuitively, Austin has been an outside receiver in the Memphis offense and hasn't been pumped screens. That showed at the Senior Bowl where he earned the highest grade of any receiver throughout the week of practices. Memphis, TN
pros: As sudden a receiver as you'll see in the draft class. Gets to top speed in a flash Crafty route-runner. Far more than a one-trick gadget guy. Not much "fake" production on tape. 90.5% of routes in 2021 came on outside.
cons: Tiny for any position. Going to get tossed around by contact at the next level. Needs to vary speed better on vertical tree. Won't use acceleration to his advantage. Shies away from any contact. Struggles to even initiate to swat hands away.
where_wins: EX P LOSIV EN ESS Everything Austin does looks like it's been put in fast forward. A lot of guys can look like that in a straight line, but Austin has that kind of ability in everything he does.
what_role: MOV EA BLE G A DG ET Austin is quite obviously going to be limited by his catch radius. That being said, he can still mismatches and big windows for quarterbacks if given a creative role. And he's also a terror with the ball in his hands.
what_improve: CA T CH P OIN T Austin simply can't fill a normal role in the NFL without getting stronger at the catch point. The windows won't be nearly as big and he'll have to deal with contact better to produce.
bottom_line: Austin has the kind of physical prowess that can overcome his size, but he's not ever going to fill a traditional role.

blurb: Austin flat out couldn't see the field his first three years on campus. D. Peoples Pompano Beach, FL
pros: Can be a bully at the catch point. Majority of contested catches came well downfield. Rocked up build. Barely an ounce of fat on him. Ascending in a big way. Made massive strides from the beginning to end of 2021.
cons: Struggles to avoid contact. Always seemingly playing through arms. Speed on tape does not match testing numbers. Rare to see him run away from corners. Upright in his route breaks. Crispness in his breaks isn't there.
where_wins: CA T CH P OIN T With ideal size and musculature, Austin often outmanned college corners at the catch point. He led all of college football with nine contested catches on deep targets.
what_role: P R OJECT X The size is there. The movement skills are there. The physicality is there. The refinement is not. The fact that Austin still needs polish after four years, however, is worrisome.
what_improve: F U N CT ION A L A T H LET ICISM Austin's testing numbers suggest that he quite clearly has the capability to change directions like an athlete, but when he was running routes on tape that didn't show up.
bottom_line: Austin's uncommon late-career breakout and athleticism testing makes him an intriguing prospect for a late-round flier.

blurb: When Rondale Moore went down for the season back in 2019, true freshman David Bell filled in as the lead dog in the Purdue offense. He went for over 1,000 yards that season and hasn't looked back since. Long- tenured Iowa coach Kirk Ferentz called Bell one of the best receivers he's ever coached against, and it's not hard to see why after Bell put up 240 yards against Iowa last season. As you'll see on his combine page, Bell is going to be quite the case study of production vs. tape vs. physical tools. Indianapolis, IN
pros: Game comes easy to him. Processes and executes like it's second nature. Thick lower half. Cornerbacks just bounce off him after the catch. Everyone knew he was the only option at Purdue, and he still produced.
cons: No second gear. Cornerbacks make up ground on him too easily. Could stand to initiate contact more along his routes prior to the catch point. So much production on contested catches. Doesn't have the size to continue that in NFL.
where_wins: N A T U R A L R ECEIV IN G A BILIT Y Bell wins with an outstanding natural receiver feel. He knows how to gain leverage and exploit that with his size. He may not be particularly dynamic, but he can still turn 6 yards into 10 after the catch.
what_role: P H Y SICA L Z Bell is a nice complementary piece in an offense. He can line up anywhere and not be out of place — that's a No. 2 or high-end No. 3 type of receiver.
what_improve: SU DDEN N ESS I'm not sure there's much room for improvement in the areas Bell is lacking. His modest physical tools are what's keeping him from being higher on draft boards.
bottom_line: Bell ticks a ton of boxes you want to see for the position, but he doesn't profile as a consistent downfield separator at the next level.

blurb: It's easy to fall in love with what Burks could be, but let's focus on what he is at the moment. He was the focal point of Arkansas's offense and their leading receiver every year he was on campus. If Arkansas ran a screen or schemed a target, it was going to Burks. Because of that, he 1-2 accounted for 37.2% of Arkansas' receiving yards the past two seasons. He was a man amongst boys, as defensive backs bounced off his 225-pound frame after the catch and at the catch point routinely. Warren, AR
pros: Size-speed demon. He's 225 pounds, and you still won't catch him from behind. Shrugs off would-be tacklers as if he didn't even feel them. Powerful lower half. Wants to play a physical brand of football. Initiates contact.
cons: Only 39 snaps vs. press coverage in 2021. Untested in that regard. Body type of an X receiver but never played there — 77% of career snaps came in slot. A touch stiff. Takes a few gather steps to throttle down at the top of a route.
where_wins: SIZ E- SP EED Burks is a vertical-route weapon. He can not only win with speed by stacking opposing corners, but he can also win regularly at the catch point when he doesn't create separation.
what_role: P R OJECT X / BIG SLOT While he played slot in college, you're drafting Burks highly to be the guy who can win outside one-on-one and where it matters most: downfield and in the red zone. Big slot is his fallback position.
what_improve: R OU T E N U A N CE Burks can still improve in a number of ways as a route-runner, mainly because he didn't run a a varied set of routes for Arkansas.
bottom_line: Burks is a traits projection. You don't find his combination of size, speed and ball skills every day.

blurb: Dixon has five years of production now to hang his hat on with nearly 4,000 career yards to his name. He's been Nicholls State's leading receiver for each of the past four seasons. Dixon's postives and negatives are so well defined on tape that it makes him a fairly clear projection to the NFL. He's an easy moving venus fly trap at the position the way he catches everything in his vicinity. While not a vertical threat, he can still separate a little. New Orleans, LA
pros: Long, rangy build. 6-foot-2, but with 6-foot-6 wingspan. Barrels off the line with good urgency for a bigger receiver. Easy hands catcher that secures passes on the move without breaking stride.
cons: Slender frame that needs to fill out more once he gets to the league. A touch high through his breaks. Rounding routes not uncommon. Not the kind of speed that will worry NFL corners.
where_wins: NA
what_role: NA
what_improve: NA
bottom_line: Dixon is a fluid mover with natural receiving skills that won't look out of place in an NFL rotation.

blurb: After playing a smaller role as a freshman and sophomore, Dotson rose to No. 1 status in the Penn State offense in 2020. Dotson is one of the few 5-foot-11 receivers who's heralded for his catch radius. His highlight reel can stretch as long as any receiver's in this draft class. Despite his limited size, he's 2-3 always been an outside receiver for the Nittany Lions. The questions with him will revolve around his playstyle translating at such a light weight. Nazareth, PA
pros: Sudden and decisive route-runner. Not a lot of wasted motion. Flare for the acrobatic catch. Has a 5.2% drop rate over his career. Terrific vision with the ball in his hands. He turns into a punt returner in space.
cons: Not the size that profiles to the outside, although he has long arms for his height. Struggled to stack corners who get hands on him. Speed is good, not great. On the older side for top WR prospect (22 on draft day). Didn't breakout until junior.
where_wins: SU DDEN N ESS Dotson not only wins with his ability to cut on dimes but also by hauling in everything thrown his way. That kind of combination will earn a quarterback's trust early on in his career.
what_role: R ELIA BLE SLOT Dotson is really tailor-made to play slot in today's NFL. He's as shifty as it gets with enough speed to challenge vertically. But, more importantly, he has a massive catch radius for a player listed at only 5-foot-11.
what_improve: MU SCLE MA SS Dotson could stand to add muscle to his frame and develop a more diverse release package. Being able to dictate terms at the line would take his game to the next level.
bottom_line: If you want a plug-and-play slot receiver, you won't find better in the draft class.

blurb: Doubs has been featured in the Nevada offense ever since he was a freshman in 2018, but his production didn't take off until quarterback Carson Strong did. He went from primarily a deep threat in 2020 to more of a well-rounded focal point of the offense in 2021. Despite his size, Doubs has struggled at the catch point, going only 28-for-68 on contested catches throughout his career. Hands haven't really been an issue for him otherwise — 5.8% career drop rate. Los Angeles, CA
pros: Long-strider who can cook when he gets going. He is a real-deal deep threat. Tremendous feet and balance. Probably runs a mean ladder drill. Employs a gorgeous shimmy release. Works it to both sides.
cons: Not an enforcer despite size. Middling contested-catch numbers over career. Ran hot and cold this past season. Not a consistent weekly focal point of the offense. Can get caught playing high. Has the ability to sink but can get lackadaisical.
where_wins: BU ILD U P SP EED After playing primarily as a deep threat in 2020, Doubs showed he could win all over the field this past season.
what_role: R A N G EY DOWN F IELD T H R EA T Doubs doesn't really have any physical limitations that stop him from playing the X role in the league as he did in college. The question is simply, can he deal with the bump in physicality?
what_improve: ST R ON G ER H A N DS Doubs has to be better at the catch point. He should have been Mossing corners left and right, considering who he was playing. It's only going to get harder at the next level.
bottom_line: Doubs has a lot of traits you look for in a receiver, but it remains to be seen if his trump-card downfield ability will translate against better competition.

blurb: Heiligh first cracked the starting lineup as a sophomore in 2019. He led the Chanticleers in receiving yards that season and every year since. While he won at every level of the field, Heiligh did his best work at the intermediate range with catches for 659 yards there. If he's going to 7-UDFA win anywhere in the NFL, that's where it's going to be. Venice, FL
pros: Loose lower half capable of running full route tree. Able to stop at a moment's notice and send defenders flying by. Legit production on a per route basis. Over 3.4 yards per route the past two seasons.
cons: Such a limited athlete. Will struggle mightily with a competition leap. Racked up production on one-cut routes vs. off coverage. Not very translateable. Doesn't use size to his advantage. Game you'd expect from smaller receiver.
where_wins: NA
what_role: NA
what_improve: NA
bottom_line: Heiligh is going to have an uphill climb separating in the NFL with limited physical tools.

blurb: Johnson started his career at Iowa State where he struggled to see the football field for two seasons before transferring to Tulsa. It was a slow build up there for two seasons before his massive breakout in 2021 that eclipsed his entire career totals prior to that. While Johnson comes with the biggest ball- skills red flag in the draft class, it's worth noting that his drop rate has decreased every single year to a somewhat palatable 8.6% in 2021. Maumelle, AR
pros: Electric make-you-miss ability. Both as a route- runner and with the ball. Varies speeds to manipulate defenders on his routes so well. Feet that can get off the line of scrimmage with ease.
cons: Disastrous drop issues. Body catcher with 13.8% career drop rate. Doesn't have the juice to take the top off of defenses. Limited vertical weapon. Slight frame. Not a physical aspect to his repertoire.
where_wins: NA
what_role: NA
what_improve: NA
bottom_line: Johnson can flat out get open. I don't care the competition level. Now him actually securing the football is another story entirely.

blurb: London played both football and basketball as a freshman at USC before the pandemic hit and turned his attention to football full-time. That's a good thing because his skill set improved by leaps and bounds over the past year and a half. He went from a skinny swing guard who played primarily in the slot to a rocked-up power forward who dominated from the outside this past season. London was on pace for a sure-fire Biletnikoff Award-winning season before he broke his ankle against Arizona. Moorpark, CA
pros: Man among boys. Dominant physicality that will still be there in the NFL. Loose hips for a tall receiver. Can legitimately shake defensive backs. Unparalleled catch radius. Remarkable body control at his size.
cons: Lacks speed. Not going to run past corners. Suffered season-ending broken ankle in October. Dropped eight of his 96 catchable targets in 2021.
where_wins: BA SKET BA LL BA CKG R OU N D London wins the way elite power forwards win — not surprising with his basketball background. He's too quick for bigger corners and too physical for smaller corners. Even when he's covered, London is still likely to haul it in.
what_role: T R U E #1 - X London is the prototypical possession receiver. He will command double-teams on third down at the next level because of how many ways he can win. Teams that use receivers heavily as blockers in the run game will covet him.
what_improve: SP EED Speed is the only real knock on his game. Sadly, I don't think that's anything he can drastically change overnight.
bottom_line: London's going to be a 100-catch, 10-touchdown-a-season guy sooner rather than later.

blurb: Melton has been a starter ever since his second year at Rugers in 2018. In 2019, he led the Scarlett Knights in targets and has done so in every season since. He's a speedster who never quite had a quarterback that could maximize that ability. In his five-years of playing time, Melton managed only 26 deep receptions. For a player with his caliber of speed, that's borderline criminal. After garnering a Senior Bowl invite, he qualified as a riser with his performance of the week of practice. Egg Harbor City, NJ
pros: Speedster that can threaten on linear routes. manual. Doesn't tap into his juice. Sets up leverage on posts/corners well. Where a lot of his explosive plays came. Well-built despite being on shorter side. Can shrug off arm-tackles.
cons: Unnatural route-runner. Like he's following a History of drops. 9.4% rate for his career. Wholly unproductive in career. 642 yards was single season high (166 on screens)
where_wins: NA
what_role: NA
what_improve: NA
bottom_line: Maybe the biggest red flag for Melton is his lack of production despite off- the-charts pre-draft testing.

blurb: Like seemingly every other Alabama receiver to come out in recent years, Metchie runs routes like they are second nature. That's been the case ever since he assumed the No. 2 role in the offense as a sophomore in 2020 after Jaylen Waddle went down. He's a natural separator, as 752 of his 1,142 yards last season came when he was deemed open by PFF's charting (14th most in FBS). He took a leap forward in terms of play strength this year, which is illustrated by the fact that he went from five broken tackles in 2020 to 20 this past season. Hightstown, NJ
pros: Crafty as can be. A true salesman with his routes. Advanced release package. Doesn't let opposing corners into his numbers. Drastically improved his YAC ability from 2020 to 2021.
cons: Tore ACL in CFP Semifinal. Lacks any high-end physical tools. Uninspiring athletic profile. Not a physical player. Gets boxed out of his routes against big corners.
where_wins: R OU T E- R U N N IN G Metchie — like pretty much every Alabama receiver in recent memory — wins with route- running IQ. To be as advanced as he is for only a true junior coming out is impressive.
what_role: SLOT The worry is Metchie has to be a slot in the NFL. With limited speed and catch radius for an outside receiver, he's a No. 2 at best at the next level.
what_improve: H EA LT H There aren't many avenues for Metchie to improve because most of his negatives are physical. It's unlikely that will improve during his ACL recovery.
bottom_line: While Metchie is pro-ready in a lot of ways, there's reason to think he's also close to capped out.

blurb: Despite never playing wide receiver in high school, Moore has been producing ever since his true freshman year at Western Michigan. He recorded 802 yards in that season before amassing just 391 in only five games during the COVID-shortened season. Despite being productive, Moore didn't look anywhere close to the guy we saw lead the FBS in broken tackles this past season. He would have been a late Day prospect on tape heading into the year, but his physical ability and comfortability at the position took a massive step forward. Pittsburgh, PA
pros: "Couldn't touch him in a phone booth" kind of agility. Special movement skills. Zero issues getting off the line of scrimmage, even against Michigan and Pittsburgh. He may be short, but he's not small. Dude is a rocked-up 195 pounds.
cons: Legit catch-radius concerns. Will show up on contested targets and off-target passes. Raw as a route-runner. Will telegraph where he's going at times. Put up massive numbers against a low level of competition. Didn't have to do much to win.
where_wins: ELU SIV EN ESS In a class with some seriously shifty wideouts, Moore would be my bet to win if they all played tag. He's not only shifty, but he's also so strong he's unaffected by an outstretch arm. That alleviates some level of competition concerns.
what_role: Y A C WEA P ON He's not a guy you want primarily on the outside, but I don't think he's slot-only, either. He can win in a number of ways, but he makes his money when featured in the underneath portion of the field.
what_improve: DEEP R OU T E T R EE Moore needs some seasoning on the intermediate and deep routes. He can already get free underneath but doesn't bring the same refinement down the field.
bottom_line: Moore has WR1 type of movement skills. His floor is a quality slot option.

blurb: Olave has been the Ohio State receiving corps' top dog ever since his true sophomore season in 2019 after Parris Campbell, Johnnie Dixon, and Terry McLaurin's exodus to the NFL. He curiously opted to return to Ohio State this past fall despite being billed as one of the most NFL- ready receiver prospects as a junior. Well, if he was NFL ready then, he damn sure is now. Olave could teach his own route- running clinic but don't expect a YAC receiver, as he's broken only nine tackles over his entire college career. San Marcos, CA
pros: Extremely polished route-runner at the deep and intermediate levels of the field. More than enough speed to separate down the field. Very sure handed. Has a 4.9% career drop rate, with most targets coming downfield.
cons: Not dynamic with the ball in his hands. Ten career broken tackles on 176 receptions. A little slimmer than you'd like. Has to keep himself clean to win. Got passed up by others in the Ohio State offense as a senior.
where_wins: R OU T E- R U N N IN G Olave wins with high-level route-running and plus speed. Leave him on an island with no help over the top too often, and you'll eventually pay.
what_role: R ELIA BLE #2 - Z Olave is your prototypical No. 2 receiver. He's not a do-it-all guy, but he's adept enough downfield that defenses can't leave him one-on-one.
what_improve: A F T ER T H E CA T CH Olave's main weakness is only that he may not be elite at anything in particular. There's not much to his game that qualifies as problematic.
bottom_line: Olave is one of the safest bets at the receiver position in the class and the perfect fit for a team that wants immediate impact at the position.

blurb: Philips broke onto the scene to become the Bruins leading receiver as a true sophomore in 2019. Unfortunately, the quarterback position for UCLA never quite improved to the point where he could see more volume in the offense. At the Shrine Bowl, however, Philips showed just how underutilized he truly was. He earned far and away the highest grade of any receiver in attendance throughout the week of practices. He's been a slot only his entire career, and that's where he profiles to in the San Marcos, CA
pros: Saucey on the underneath route tree. Short- area quicks are fantastic. Varies speeds like a vet. Knows he's not a blazer and has to lull you to sleep. Understands how to attack leverage to gain separation.
cons: Limited juice. Likely pigeonholes him to the slot. Small hands and body catching led to some drop issues over career. Skinnier frame with short arms. Smaller catch radius than you'd like even in slot.
where_wins: CR A F T IN ESS You don't want to see Philips' pattering feet bearing down on you from off-coverage. He's a precise route-runner with the kind of change of direction ability to run any route in the book.
what_role: SLOT Philips is one of the cleanest projections in the wide receiver draft class. He'll be a pure slot at the next level.
what_improve: P LA Y ST R EN G T H The truly elite pure slot options in the NFL are often built more like running backs. Taking hits and dealing with contact from linebackers is a big part of the job. Phillips has to get stronger to do those things consistently.
bottom_line: Arguably the best slot-only in the class, Philips is a good bet to still get open underneath and working the middle of the field in the NFL.

blurb: Three years ago, there wasn't much debate about who was the most likely WR1 in the 2022 draft class, as Pickens was already a man amongst boys for Georgia as a true freshman, accruing 726 yards and an 88.0 receiving grade. Unfortunately, that was as good as we'd see for Pickens. He 1-2 struggled to build rapport with a rough Georgia quarterback room as a sophomore then tore his ACL last spring before returning at the end of the year to play all of Hoover, AL
pros: Carves kids up at the catch point and has been doing it ever since he was a freshman. So good at getting late separation with subtle leans and shoulder nudges. Swats hands away consistently at the line of scrimmage and throughout the route.
cons: Very limited juice. Not the guy to take the top off a defense. On the field for only 35 pass plays this season after tearing ACL last spring. Suspended for violating team rules and kicked out of a game for fighting as a freshman in 2019.
where_wins: BA LL SKILLS Pickens' ball skills are among the best in the class. Even hobbled, he still managed to make one of the best catches in the SEC Championship and National Championship this season.
what_role: P R OJECT X Pickens looked like a shoo-in to be a WR1 in the NFL after his freshman season. He certainly has the size to stick on the outside in the NFL. That ability hasn't gone anywhere, but it comes with far more questions now.
what_improve: H EA LT H Pickens needs to show that he's developed since his tremendous true freshman campaign because we've yet to see much in that regard.
bottom_line: Pickens was quite clearly not himself after coming back from his ACL tear. His prospects will be decided in private on-field workouts and the combine.

blurb: Pierce broke onto the scene as Cincinnati's deep threat as a redshirt freshman in 2019. Three years later and he never quite blossomed into much more. His 16.8 yard career average depth of target is one of the highest in the draft class, as he's best known for striding away from defenders down the sideline. Some of that is Cincinnati's offense, but he's also far more of a linear athlete than a dynamic one. Bigger Glen Ellyn, IL
pros: Insane acceleration for a man his size. First few steps in space cover so much ground. Very quick to stack corners on the outside. Ideal traits to do so in the NFL as well. Can really go up and get it. Lot of high-polnt catches on tape. yards.
cons: Stiff route-runner. Rounded breaks are commonplace on tape. Contact jostles him more than you'd expect for a receiver his size. Why wasn't he more productive? Four years with a top QB prospect and never had 1,000
where_wins: JU ICE You'd be hard pressed to find a receiver in the FBS that stacked corners more consistently on go-balls than Pierce. His combination of size and explosiveness was simply too much for the low- level corners he faced.
what_role: V ER T ICA L T R EE SP ECIA LIST No one stacked corners on go balls more frequently than Pierce in 2021. Some of that is level of competition, but he even did it on multiple occasions against Alabama when he wasn't targeted. His size-explosiveness combo is scary.
what_improve: F U LL R OU T E T R EE Gos, slants, posts. That was 63.6% of Pierce's receiving yards in 2021. That was by design because he is not the kind of receiver to shake corners at the top of routes.
bottom_line: Pierce may never be a complete receiver, but he'll be coveted by vertical- based passing offenses.

blurb: Roberson was already on NFL radars as a candidate for the 2020 draft after a N/A tremendous redshirt sophomore campaign that saw him put up 803 yards in only eight games. Sadly, that season was cut short N/A with a foot injury which caused him to return to school. He averaged over 100 yards the 7-UDFA next year as well through four games until a torn ACL ended his season and caused him to return again. That string of bad luck didn't Slimmer subside as Roberson returned looking Jalen completely zapped of the big play Reagor explosiveness that made him so dangerous early on in his career. Mesquite, TX
pros: Play speed gear his competition level couldn't handle. No nonsense YAC weapon. Gets upfield and goes on the attack Short, but not undersized. Massive 6-foot-6 wingspan with plus play strength.
cons: Extensive injury history. 2 season ending. Undisclosed foot injury and ACL. Not a full route tree runner even at his peak. Excels on silo routes. Only 7-20 in contested situations over the past two seasons
where_wins: NA
what_role: NA
what_improve: NA
bottom_line: Roberson was a day 2 prospect when healthy. He's still worth a flier to see if he ever returns to that.

blurb: Robinson started his career at Nebraska where he was treated as a pure space athlete than a true receiver. 37 of his catches there came on screens. It wasn't until he transferred to Kentucky that he got to flourish as an all-around slot receiver. In the new look Wildcats offense, Robinson was the focal point racking up eight-plus catches in eight of their 13 contests. He hauled in 16 deep receptions after only Faster seven total in his first two seasons. Daniel Frankfort, KY
pros: Can't touch him in a phone booth kind of ability. Undersized, but very well built. A strong 178 pounds that took some licks in 2021. Not just an underneath slot guy. Speed to get vertical up the seam.
cons: Such a limited catch radius. Will have the smallest arms of any receiver in the NFL. A ton of schemed production. 35 screen receptions in 2021. Gadget guy, but not utilized as returner and had little success when he was.
where_wins: SH IMMY - SH A KIN G Robinson has that kind of bounce that everyone is looking for at the receiver position. He can make hard cuts and juke moves in space without seemingly losing a step.
what_role: SLOT - G A DG ET With the size of windows over the middle of the field in the NFL, it's going to be difficult for Robinson to replicate a lot of the production we saw from him at Kentucky. He may be limited to a screen/schemed target role.
what_improve: R OU T E P A CIN G When Robinson went vertical on tape at Kentucky, he let you know immediately off the snap with his urgency. Safeties in the NFL are too savvy and athletic to not stay on top when that's the case.
bottom_line: Robinson is an ascending slot receiver, but his limited catch radius will be a turn off for many offenses.

blurb: I can count on my hands the number of college players I've scouted over the years who legitimately peaked as a true freshman, and Ross is now one of those. He went for 1,000 yards way back in 2018 at an FBS-leading 4.98 yards per route. Since then, however, he's failed to improve. It didn't help that he missed all of 2020 with a neck injury that threatened his career and didn't have Trevor Lawrence throwing him footballs when he came back, but his lack of development is concerning. Phenix City, AL
pros: Massive wingspan. Plucks balls well outside of his frame with ease. Can sink his hips better than most 6-foot-4 receivers. Route tree won't be limited. Numbers torpedoed by inaccuracies at Clemson's quarterback position in 2021.
cons: Spinal surgery forced him to miss 2020 season and jeopardized his career. Lacks the kind of explosiveness to separate routinely. Limits him. Production peaked as a freshman and declined every year after.
where_wins: CA T CH P OIN T Ross can get off the line and create separation in short areas. From there, he presents quarterbacks with a massive target and can make up for a quarterback with shaky ball placement.
what_role: P OSSESSION WR Ross is best suited for either a "big slot" role or for a team that runs a lot of quick game. He presents mismatch potential with his height and physicality.
what_improve: MA IN T A IN IN G SIZ E A DV A N T A G E Ross isn't strong enough to maintain the brand of football he plays. He needs to be in the 220- pound range to manhandle NFL corners the way he did in college.
bottom_line: The talent he showed as a freshman didn't go anywhere, but he simply never developed more physically. You're going to have to accept his limitations.

blurb: Shakir isn't a new riser by any means, as he's been "broken out" ever since his true sophomore season back in 2019, when he barely trailed Eagles receiver John Hightower with 872 receiving yards. He has displayed a flare for the spectacular catch as well. Shakir played primarily in the slot in 2019 and 2021 but was an outside receiver in the shortened 2020 season, where he still put together some good tape. Murrieta, CA
pros: Circus-catch king. He had single games that could fill a highlight reel. Has a great kickstand move in space. Broken tackle numbers don't do it justice. Plus instincts for avoiding contact and finding holes over the middle of the field.
cons: Skinny with average speed. Not a great combo projecting to the next level. Concentration drops out the wazoo — 10 this past season alone. Slot-only for Boise State. 59 snaps vs. press coverage all season.
where_wins: BODY CON T R OL Shakir wins with body control. Whether that's at the catch point or avoiding linebackers, Shakir can contort any which way he needs to.
what_role: SLOT Shakir is likely to find a home in the slot at the next level and could push for a starting role. The confidence with which he attacks the ball is what you want at that position.
what_improve: SEP A R A T IN G DOWN F IELD Shakir has to work on varying his speeds better as a route-runner to separate down the field. He's not a burner who can win with pure juice at that level, so he needs to find other ways.
bottom_line: The highlight reel is as good as it gets, but the translateable tools leave more to be desired.

blurb: With Tolbert's receiving totals, his career progression is akin something out of a book. He went from redshirting to 50 yards, to yards, to 1,085 yards, to 1,474 yards this past season as a redshirt junior. He's always been explosive, averaging 17.0 yards per reception in each of his three years as a 2-3 starter. While the competition level wasn't ideal, Tolbert proved that he belongs during the Senior Bowl practices. Mobile, AL
pros: Not only has high-end top speed but can also get there quickly for a 6-foot-3 receiver. Long-limbed with a penchant for high-pointing footballs. Flexible lower half for a tall receiver. Capable of running full route tree.
cons: Will be 23 years old on draft day and still built like a stick. Consistently false-steps with his front foot out of his stance. Hasn't faced a Power Five opponent since 2019.
where_wins: A CCELER A T ION Tolbert wins down the football field. He accelerates extremely well for a taller wide receiver, making it imperative for corners to get hands on him.
what_role: R A N G EY DOWN F IELD T H R EA T Tolbert can immediately add a deep threat to any offense, but he's a long-term project. With a couple years of NFL coaching and NFL weight training, he could be a completely different animal.
what_improve: BET T ER COMP ET IT ION Tolbert just needs reps against better cornerbacks. He's spent years beating up guys who can't hold his jock athletically and didn't have to clean up bad habits to get open.
bottom_line: While the speed and catch radius are intriguing, Tolbert's frame and age combined with the level of competition give serious pause.

blurb: Watson was your run of the mill 0-star recruit when he showed up to North Dakota State. He put on over 20 pounds over the course of his five-years with the Bison to become the physical monster you see today. Despite middling volume stats as a starter the past three seasons, Watson was actually insanely productive on a per opportunity basis. NDSU simply didn't pass a lot. His 2.95 career yards per route run figure is one of the highest in the draft class. Tampa, FL
pros: Elite all-around athlete. One of the best pre- draft testers at the WR position ever. Incredible flexibility for a 6-foot-4 receiver. Sinks low at the line and in his breaks. Easy accelleration combined wtih long strides makes him a nightmare for corners downfield
cons: Fights the ball in the air with ugly drops all over his tape. Consistent drop issues. Doesn't use his size to his advantage. Rare to see him initiating contact. Runs routes as they're printed on the playbook. Doesn't set defenders up.
where_wins: F LEX IBLE A T H LET ICISM Most 6-foot-4 receivers struggle mightily to drop their hips at the top of routes to create the precisicison necessary to gain separation in the NFL. That's not the case with Watson who explodes in his cuts like a man much smaller.
what_role: P R OJECT X While it's all there physically to be a number one in the NFL, there's still many aspects of the receiver position where Watson is underdeveloped. He'll be a vertical threat out the gate with hopefully more in time.
what_improve: BA LL SKILLS With a 13.3% career drop rate and 30% career contested catch conversion rate, Watson has left a lot of yards on the field at the collegiate level. The question becomes, is this something that one can even improve once they get ot the NFL?
bottom_line: Watson is more athlete than wide receiver at this point. If he becomes well versed in the latter...look out.

blurb: Williams spent two years watching from the sidelines at Ohio State before transferring to Alabama and putting together one of the most explosive receiving seasons college football has ever seen. He averaged 20.0 yards per catch on 78 receptions! He's not only fast but shifty as well, which is a deadly combination when it comes to getting open. He often created separation, as 1,329 of his 1,561 yards came Taller when he was deemed open by PFF's DeSean charting — the most in college football. Jackson Saint Louis, MO
pros: Elite, angle-changing, uncatchable top speed. Don't usually see at his height. Shiftiness at the line is different for a speedster. He's both quick and fast. Sells his vertical routes by changing speeds and attacking leverage.
cons: Tore his ACL in the National Championship Game. Still rail thin for a taller receiver. Bully ball is not going to be his game. One-year wonder. Was stuck behind the Ohio State trio before transferring last summer.
where_wins: SP EED Williams is a home-run threat from anywhere with the ball in his hands. His combination of speed and YAC ability for a 6-foot-2 receiver is rare.
what_role: DEEP T H R EA T Williams is still not your true X receiver you can trust to win possession routes. He's your vertical- route specialist who can also take screens, jet sweeps, etc.
what_improve: MU SCLE MA SS Putting on some muscle would go a long way for Williams. He doesn't play timidly by any means, but he doesn't have the play strength to enforce his will at the catch point.
bottom_line: His ACL recovery obviously has to be vetted, but if you need a deep threat, don't pass on this guy.

blurb: While scouting K.J. Hill in 2019, I saw an unfamiliar Ohio State wide receiver run a blaze out with the kind of uncoachable shimmy-shake on his route break that only the elite route-runners at the position possess. Upon further investigation, I discovered it was true freshman Garrett Wilson. He put up some highlights in a limited role that season before becoming a focal point of the offense from the slot in 2020. His high-end basketball background is apparent in everything he does, and he might have the most raw talent in the receiver class. Austin, TX
pros: Insane body control. Can adjust to just about anything. Big catch radius. Stop-start and change of direction are special. Bouncy in and out of breaks. Innate feel as a ball carrier. Weapon after the catch.
cons: Not enough answers for press coverage yet. Long corners gave him issues. Gets caught too "dancy" in his routes. Throws off timing and won't fly in the NFL. Struggles with physicality in his routes. Rarely the aggressor.
where_wins: SH IF T IN ESS Wilson wins with downright filthy route-running ability. He has more plays spinning cornerbacks in circles than any receiver in this class. Give him two-way gos or option routes, and he'll win at will.
what_role: MOV A BLE WEA P ON Wilson will likely have to start his career in the slot or as the Z in an offense. Given a free release, he's the best in the class at manipulating defenders in space.
what_improve: P LA Y ST R EN G T H Wilson flat out has to get stronger. He possesses rare traits at the receiver position but risks being pigeonholed in the slot at the next level if his play strength doesn't improve.
bottom_line: Wilson has a ton of uncoachable tools to work with, but in certain ways, he is more of a project than we're used to seeing out of Ohio State.
