blurb: Bellinger has been starting ever since his sophomore season for the Aztecs. He's steadily been featured more and more in the San Diego State offense every single year but never quite as a downfield weapon. Of his 31 receptions this past season, only four came 10-plus yards down the field. It really is a shame we didn't get to see more of him in such a role, as he has the physical tools to win there at the next Las Vegas, NV
pros: Sure handed. Didn't drop a ball in 2021 and only 4.2% drop rate for career. Willing blocker with three years of starting experience in pro-style concepts and usage. Plus speed and get-off at the line for the position. Can threaten on crossers.
cons: No creativity on his route breaks. Only gets open by initiating contact. Linear player after the catch. Lacks wiggle. Afterthrought in the passing attack. Insanely low 3.7 yard average depth of target.
where_wins: R ELIA BILIT Y With strong hands, large frame, and plus play strength, Bellinger should provide a reliable target at the next level.
what_role: IN LIN E T E You can get away with Bellinger as your starter at the next level and not have to limit your playbook.
what_improve: CR EA T IV IT Y There's just not much on Bellinger's tape that excites. He's obviously a plus athlete, but the reps you notice that are few and far between.
bottom_line: There aren't too many weaknesses in Bellinger's game, but there aren't many trump cards either.

blurb: Calcaterra started his career at Oklahoma where he saw the field right out the gate with 10 catches for 162 yards and three scores as a true freshman. His 12 catch, 396 yard, score sophomore campaign in 2018 put him firmly on NFL radars as a potential top tight end in the 2020 draft. Tragically, concussion symptoms caused him to miss the second half of 2019 and then prematurely retire from football altogether. After sitting out an entire he, Calcaterra decided to return to the game and join another former Sooner in quarterback Tanner Mordecai at SMU. Rancho Santa Margarita, CA
pros: Very fluid mover for the position. Like a rocked up wide out. On the shorter side, but with broad shoulder and well-sized catch radius still Capable of running a full NFL route tree. Speed to work vertical as well.
cons: Inline blocking was an afterthought at both stops. 15.9% career inline rate. Average ball skills for the position. Not the level of reliability you'd like. Has already retired from football.
where_wins: NA
what_role: NA
what_improve: NA
bottom_line: Calcaterra's concussion history will scare teams off. As a pure pass catcher with no other concerns he'd go multiple rounds higher than this.

blurb: Deese started off his career at Golden West College before transferring to San Jose N/A State. After redshirting his first year with the Spartans in 2018, Deese didn't gain much traction in his first two years of playing time N/A until his breakout 720-yard campaign last fall. Deese has split his time evenly between 7-UDFA the slot and inline over the course of his career and has shown more than enough as a blocker to succeed there in the Slower league. It's his receiving ability that still Jerrell leaves a lot to be desired. His best bet may Adams come as a full-back in the NFL. La Palma, CA
pros: Plays a physical brand of football. As a blocker and pass catcher. 6-foot-3 with an expansive 6-foot-9 wingspan. Large catch radius. Carries a lot of weight in his ass and thighs. Helps him to still be a plus blocker.
cons: No suddenness to his routes. Does not profile to a separator in the NFL. Unreliable hands. Drop rate a shade over 10% in his career. Nothing special after the catch. Nine career broken tackles on 86 catches.
where_wins: NA
what_role: NA
what_improve: NA
bottom_line: Deese is the rare undersized tight end that could likely hack it as a blocker still in the league. He's just not the athlete to justify it, though.

blurb: Dulcich showed up to UCLA as a well undersized preferred walk-on. He's completely remade his body and his game in the years since. He broke out in a starting role with 517 yards in only seven games back in 2020 but has put on nearly pounds even since then. If he played with a better quarterback situation this past season, he could have pushed for around 1,000 yards with how often he was open on La Canada Flintridge, CA
pros: Understands how to set up defenders. Very natural receiver. Terrific at avoiding contact. Uses feet and hands in unison to do so. Enough speed to challenge every level of the defense.
cons: Still thin. Build trends closer to a receiver than NFL tight end on tape. Wide hands gets him rocked back too often as a run blocker. Hitch and spot routes need refining. Comes in too high and exaggerates turn.
where_wins: N A T U R A L R ECEIV IN G A BILIT Y Dulcich is the kind of athlete that could still produce if he lost 20 pounds and just played wide receiver. He's got that kind of feel and body control to separate.
what_role: R ECEIV IN G T E Dulcich will never be a plus blocker in the NFL, but he's at least respectable in that regard. Dulcich will be coveted for his all-around receiving ability that can work from any alignment.
what_improve: MU SCU LA T U R E Dulcich has already come a long way from the 210-pounder that showed up at UCLA, but he shouldn't be done yet. Dulcich has 5-10 pounds more to go before he's ready to be a high-level contributor in the NFL.
bottom_line: Dulcich has arguably the best feel for getting open at the tight end position in the class, but just needs to get a little bigger.

blurb: Ferguson has been on the NFL's radar ever since his impressive redshirt freshman campaign that saw him catch 36 balls for 456 yards in 2018. He simply never progressed physically from that year. After being listed at an undersized 239 pounds that year, three years past and Ferguson was only listed five pounds heavier last fall. The worry about his tapped out frame isn't unwarranted, but even at that size his play style should survive in the league. Madison, WI
pros: Strong hands at the catch point. 58.3% contested catch rate for career. Very natural with the ball in his hands. 32 career broken tackles. Tons of inline experience on pro-style run concepts.
cons: Speed is very limited. Small route tree that he can succeed on in the NFL. Penalized seven times this past season. Willing and experienced inline blocker, but bulk is below-average to do so in NFL.
where_wins: NA
what_role: NA
what_improve: NA
bottom_line: Ferguson is a reliable and movable number 2 tight end that can work in the red zone.

blurb: Kolar hit it big as a redshirt sophomore in 2019 when he racked up 51 catches for 697 yards as Brock Purdy's de facto top option in Hakeem Butler's absence. Despite that top-notch production, Kolar eschewed the NFL for not one, but two more seasons with the Cyclones. He's been much the same guy ever since. That same guy, though, has produced at a heck of a high level for a collegiate tight end. Norman, OK
pros: Outstanding at the catch point. Was pumped contested targets because of how good he is. Has mastered the art of the subtle shove at the top of routes. Only five drops on 174 catchable his entire career.
cons: Will not be able to avoid contact in the NFL. Swallowed up routinely already. Tips the scales over 250, but on his long frame that's still less than ideal muscle mass. Glorified slot receiver in Iowa State's offense. Inline blocking is work in progress.
where_wins: NA
what_role: NA
what_improve: NA
bottom_line: Kolar is the best "even when he's not open, he's open" tight end in the class. That will play in the red zone.

blurb: Every year, there is a "move" tight end who needs to put weight to actually stick in the NFL. Likely is that guy in 2022. Few tight ends can hold a candle to his production, as he averaged 2.42 yards per route for his career. Flip on the tape, though, and you may not even be able to distinguish him size-wise from the rest of Coastal Carolina's receivers. It didn't help that he almost exclusively blocked in space or at the second level of the defense. He's a projection but is already adding weight to his frame. Maiden, MA
pros: Advanced route-runner. Sets up defenders with his stems. Runs routes outside regularly. Bridges the gap between tight end and receiver. Speed to easily outrun linebackers. He even ran away from safeties at times.
cons: Not the size of an NFL tight end. Won't get respected in the run game. Even when in-line, Likely was used almost exclusively as a second-level blocker. A lot of schemed production in unique Coastal Carolina offense.
where_wins: N A T U R A L R ECEIV IN G A BILIT Y Likely is one heck of a natural receiver. He attacks the ball so well in the air and can create on his own after the catch.
what_role: MOV E T E This is the tricky thing. He's not quite dynamic enough to pass as a receiver and not big enough to be respected as a tight end. He's a move tight end in a league that doesn't use them anymore.
what_improve: SIZ E This one is obvious, Likely has to get bigger. The big question is, can he? He's almost indistinguishable from a wide receiver on tape with his frame. He's in no-man's land at the tight end position at his current weight.
bottom_line: Likely just has to get bigger and stronger. He can be a difference-maker if he can maintain his athleticism with 15 more pounds.

blurb: There haven't been many offenses in college football history more tight end focused than Colorado State's over the past two years. Over that span, McBride accounted for 38.1% of the Rams' passing yards — an insane market share for any position, let alone tight end. He debated transferring during the pandemic after a breakout 45-catch, 560-yard sophomore campaign but decided to return and has ascended to TE1 status nonetheless. Fort Morgan, CO
pros: Strides past linebackers easily. More than enough speed to test the seams. Put up rare numbers in college. He was the focal point of Colorado State's offense. Ran diverse and translatable route tree.
cons: Not going to be a move tight end, nor will he win one-on-one outside despite doing so in college. Straight-line, after-the-catch player. Not much dynamism. Man among boys at his level of competition.
where_wins: DOWN F IELD McBride wins where so few tight ends do — down the football field. He can get past the linebacker-level swiftly and then presents a massive target over the middle. He can do it all while also being a respectable blocker.
what_role: A LL- A R OU N D T E McBride is a starting in-line tight end from Day 1. The leap in competition obviously presents a learning curve, but he's talented and proven enough to not stress about it.
what_improve: P H Y SICA L R OU T ES McBride could stand to get even more physical as a route-runner. He's too content with someone hanging on him at times, knowing he's likely to win at the catch point, which won't always be the case in the league.
bottom_line: McBride has already excelled in a high-usage role, as expected when drafting him highly. However, he just doesn't quite look like Kyle Pitts athletically.

blurb: Mitchell was a hit as a sophomore in when he proved to be one of the best big play tight ends in the country. He averaged 17.2 yards per reception that season. With Dalton Keene out of the picture in 2020, Mitchell started to get featured more while still maintaining a high 17.3 yards per reception average. WIth high hopes for his draft potential in 2021, Mitchell would unfortunately go down with a torn ACL in their week 2 game against Middle Tennessee State. Big Stone Gap, VA
pros: Extensive experience running comprehensive route tree. Route running chops of a former WR. Burst pops off the tape. Both off the line and after the catch. Gets down and dirty in the run game. Rare TE that looks to finish.
cons: Not a true box out tight end who'll make plays with defenders draped on him. Approaches simple routes - crossers, flats, etc. - nonchalantly at times. Torn ACL ended his 2021 season two games in.
where_wins: NA
what_role: NA
what_improve: NA
bottom_line: Mitchell is the forgotten man in the tight end class after tearing his ACL, but when healthy his receiving tape was up there with anyone's in the class.

blurb: A popular coaching mantra is "control what you can control," and that 100% applies to Cade Otton's tape, as he was wasted in a rough Washington offense over the past few years. That being said, he still brought it every chance he had, especially as a run-blocker, where he's among the most versatile in the class. He never received more than 43 targets in a season despite being TE1 in Washington since 2019. Otton was used mainly underneath — 6.8- yard average depth of target — throughout his career. Olympia, WA
pros: Can create on his own after the catch. Knows to get upfield quickly. Feisty in the run game. He is just OK in-line one- on-one but exceptional on the move. Well-proportioned 250 pounds. Holds it with ease while still being an athlete.
cons: He is "just a guy" athletically. Not sure he has any plus traits. Not a downfield threat. Has only 23 career catches on passes 10-plus yards downfield. Average size to get by on blocking prowess alone.
where_wins: WILLIN G N ESS IN R U N G A ME Otton wins in the running game. With tight ends wearing a lot of hats as run-blockers nowadays, Otton is perfectly suited to fill whatever role asked of him in the run game.
what_role: V ER SA T ILE BLOCKER Diverse run games will love being able to deploy this guy. Otton has the want, size and technique to be a difference-maker in this regard while also being a respectable receiver.
what_improve: SEP A R A T IN G DOWN F IELD This is a tough question for Otton because the things keeping him from being a top prospect are physical in nature and not likely to be fixed anytime soon.
bottom_line: You'll have to accept physical limitations, but he has value as a blocker at tight end or even fullback in an offense.

blurb: Surrounded by three likely first-round receivers at Ohio State, Ruckert knew his role in the offense and played it admirably. Ruckert is, first and foremost, a run-blocker, as he's averaged less than one yard per route for his career despite starting the past three seasons. That being said, he's arguably the best run-blocker in the draft class. His 14 big-time blockers are the third most of any FBS tight end over the past two years despite only playing in eight games in Lindenhurst, NY
pros: Legitimate people-mover in the running game. Recorded nine big-time blocks in 2021. Built like a block of granite. Rocked-up frame. zone-beater type. Bulldozer post-catch. He will bounce defensive backs off the turf.
cons: Afterthought in the passing game. Saw three targets a game on average. No juice as a route-runner — he's really just a Needs to play with more control as a run- blocker. Gets helmet ahead of toes at times.
where_wins: N A ST IN ESS Ruckert will be coveted because of his work in the run game. He blends security-blanket receiving traits with some bone-crushing run blocks.
what_role: BLOCKIN G T E Ruckert has prototypical blocking-tight end traits to be a TE2 in an offense. He could also start for offenses that don't ask tight ends to do much more than underneath routes in the passing game.
what_improve: OV ER EX T EN DIN G Ruckert still tends to get overextended going for the kill shot in the run game. That will become more of an issue in the NFL. In the passing game, the dude just needs reps.
bottom_line: Ruckert is a plug-and-play in-line blocker but is more of a placeholder than difference-maker in the passing game.

blurb: Woods started off his career as a quarterback at Oklahoma State before moving to tight end. There he was an afterthought in the Cowboys passing attack for three seasons. So much so that he was left in to pass protect on 228 of the passing snaps he was on the field. Woods 3-4 then transferred to Virginia where he blossomed as a pass catcher. He showed a unique ability to separate downfield, and his 11.1 yard average depth of target was indicative of that. Ellenwood, GA
pros: Gargantuan frame - even for a tight end. Massive target over the middle of the field. Explodes off the line for a man his size. Can get to safeties in a hurry. Rocked up frame. Defenders melt off him. project.
cons: Awkward gate and unwillingness to get low leads to him telegraphing routes too often. Body catcher with 10.7% drop rate in his career. Will turn 24 as a rookie. Concerning age for a
where_wins: T OOLS You won't find a more impressive specimen at the tight end position at this class. There sure haven't been many comparable athletes at his size. He's still a ball of physical clay waiting to be molded.
what_role: SEA M R IP P ER Woods is tailor-made to threaten the seams of opposing defenses. He can fly off the line and present a massive window for quarterbacks to hit. That's a big value add in the NFL.
what_improve: R OU T E- R U N N IN G Woods is a physical specimen for sure, but if he runs any route at the moment that asks him to do more than put one foot in the ground and explode it can be rough.
bottom_line: Woods may take a while to put it all together, but his speed and catch radius can play from day one.

blurb: True freshman tight ends typically don't produce the way Wydermyer did back in 2019, when he caught 32 passes for yards and six scores. The worrisome thing is that he hasn't improved that statline much in the years since. Despite ideal size for the position, Wydermyer never developed ideal athleticism. In fact, his eight broken tackles as a true freshman are still a career high. He's still a very natural receiver but has never offered much as a blocker. Dickinson, TX
pros: Very fluid big man. Shows up when he adjusts course on the fly. Consistently elusive after the catch. Comfortable with the ball in his hands. Flexible at the top of routes. Will be tough to guard on option routes in the league.
cons: Doesn't have the killer instinct as a run blocker, even when attacking DBs. Far too many drops for a chain-mover type. Nearly 10% drop rate for career. Middling athlete by NFL standards. Speed leaves something to be desired.
where_wins: LOOSE H IP S Wydermyer wins with his loose route-running ability. He can run a full route tree for the tight end position and not look out of place, which he pairs with a large catch radius.
what_role: R ECEIV IN G T E Wydermyer isn't quite a plug-and-play guy. He can make an impact as a receiver to start, but you're investing in what he can be long term if you draft him.
what_improve: WILLIN G N ESS IN R U N G A ME Wydermyer has to show more "want to" as a run blocker. On tape, he's content being in position and playing patty cake. That won't fly in the NFL.
bottom_line: Wydermyer is still a project in a number of ways, but he offers traits you rarely see from a man his size.

blurb: After redshirting his freshman year in 2017, Bruss has been seeing the field for the Badgers ever since. He made spot starts down the stretch in 2018 at right tackle before taking over as the starting right tackle in 2019. After moving to right guard in the shortened 2020 season, Bruss was back at right tackle in 2021 where he had a career year. Guard is still likely where he ends up in the NFL, but that cross-training will serve him well. Kimberly, WI
pros: Plus athlete for the position that can locate well off combo blocks. Balance to recover blocks when they aren't clean. Won't see him on the floor often. Only five penalties over the course of his entire college caerer.
cons: Won't keep his base into blocks on the move. Plays less agile than he has because of it. Won't always utilize his length. Let's defenders into pads too often. Average drive in his lower half. Won't move the line of scrimmage in the NFL.
where_wins: NA
what_role: NA
what_improve: NA
bottom_line: Bruss is a scheme diverse guard with tackle versatility that should be a starter sooner rather than later.

blurb: Cross was a former top recruit who was thrown to the fire in a big way when Mike Leach took over in 2020. He went from pass-blocking snaps in 2019 to 574 in 2020. He struggled a bit, understandably, allowing 44 pressures. But as a redshirt sophomore in 2021, Cross showed up a different animal. Top-10 He only allowed 16 pressures, and his run blocking prowess took a gigantic step forward. He still hasn't done a ton of NFL concepts in the run game, which should be a steep learning curve in the league. Laurel, MS
pros: Super light on his feet. Upper-echelon mirror ability. Uses his length really well. Punch timing and placement are pluses. Progressed year over year and even improved as 2021 season went on.
cons: Inexperienced in pro-style run blocking concepts. All base zone blocks. Needs to get more consistent depth in his pass sets. Unique stance with feet really tight together, leading to massive first steps.
where_wins: LEN G T H Cross has prototypical traits to be a blindside pass protector. His feet, length and core strength are all top notch. He's been in pass protection a ton over the past two seasons.
what_role: LEF T T A CKLE Cross is a left tackle. There will likely be a learning curve early on but get this guy on the football field.
what_improve: F OOT WOR K The most encouraging thing for Cross is that he can still improve a lot of areas within his skill set. He graded very well despite inconsistent footwork.
bottom_line: Cross has the most impressive pass-blocking toolbox in the class. It may take time, but everything is there.

blurb: Deculus is the rare four-year starter at a blue blood program in the SEC that really never registered on NFL radars. He's got an NFL frame, but not quite NFL caliber physical ability. It's a big reason why he saw his grade plateau over his five years at LSU. Sadly, I'm not sure there's a next level in 7-UDFA Deculus' development to be had and a move inside to guard isn't going to alleviate his problems. Cypress, TX
pros: Idea size/length to stick at tackle in the NFL. trouble. Very high in pass sets. Can fire out of his stance and gain depth to match speed in pass protection. Independent hand usage in his sets that's NFL- ready.
cons: Stiffness to his lower half that gets him in serious Get's push-pulled like clockwork when technique isn't perfect. Won't outleverage defensive ends at the point of attack.
where_wins: NA
what_role: NA
what_improve: NA
bottom_line: Deculus is battle-tested in the SEC, but never quite won those battles frequently enough to excite.

blurb: Diesch has one unique build for the tackle position at 6-foot-7, barely scraping 300 pounds and with oddly short 32 1/4-inch arms. But, if you can get past that, you'll find one heck of a pass-protector. He is one of the smoothest-moving tackle prospects in the draft class and has never allowed more than two pressures in a single game, even if his career has been brief. He couldn't lock down a starting role in four seasons at Texas A&M before transferring to Arizona State, where his 2020 season lasted all of four Trophy Club, TX
pros: Moves like an athlete in space. This is the guy you want leading a screen. Hands are ultra quick to reset and regain leverage. Plays with a tremendous base as a run-blocker and alleviates some size issues.
cons: So slim even after years upon years in college weight rooms. Looks like a tight end. No pop to his punch. Hands can be swatted away too easily. Sixth-year senior coming out.
where_wins: F EET Diesch can consistently gain the upper hand on defenders due to his nimble feet and quick first step. He's never going to be a people mover but can still be effective.
what_role: SWIN G T A CKLE Diesch is an investment who could pay off big dividends. He's either a left tackle or not seeing the field. The best fit for him is an outside zone scheme due to his athleticism.
what_improve: SIZ E Diesch has the frame and athleticism to pass protect at the NFL level, but none of the play strength. He can't see a field until he gets stronger.
bottom_line: If a team can get his play strength to even a serviceable NFL level, Diesch can be a starting left tackle in the NFL.

blurb: You won't find too many top-10 draft picks who once held offers from Harvard coming out of high school, but Ekwonu will soon be one of them. You also won't find too many true juniors who can throw around 250-plus- pounders the way Ekwonu did last year, but that's something he's been doing ever since Top-10 he was a freshman back in 2019. His pass- blocking prowess earlier in his career led some to think he'd have to kick inside to guard, but after seeing the strides he made in 2021, he's firmly a tackle in the NFL. Charlotte, NC
pros: Biggest bully in college football. Defenders don't want to see him coming their way. Long arms that pack a punch. If he's latched onto your pads, good luck. Incredible power in his lower half. Legs like tree trunks.
cons: Pass sets are wholly inconsistent and unpolished. Almost clicks his heels. Didn't even take vertical sets, just angle sets. Agility and mirror ability are just OK and not high end for the position.
where_wins: P OWER He wins with prodigious power throughout his frame. When he uncoils his hips into contact, defenders move backward. It's just physics due to the amount of force he's capable of generating.
what_role: T A CKLE- G U A R D I wouldn't argue with teams that see him as a guard because of how nasty he is in a phone booth. This guy can stay at left tackle, though, and should be given every opportunity to succeed there.
what_improve: P A SS SET S His pass sets need to be completely reworked. His base is very inconsistent, and he has limited answers for pass-rushers at the moment. Ekwonu definitely has the physical capability to clean all that up, though.
bottom_line: Any run-heavy team should have this guy as OT1. He's a work in progress in pass protection, but his issues are very fixable.

blurb: Eze grew up playing basketball and didn't play football until his junior year of high school. He quickly took to the game and started garnering offers from blue-blood programs. Not quite understanding the college football landscape, Eze eventually committed to Memphis because he liked their coaches the best. After four years there - two as a starter - Eze transferred to TCU to face better competition and he still showed out in pass protection at left tackle. Nashville, TN
pros: Insanely long arms. Like an octopus enveloping it's prey. Basketball background shows in his pass sets. Not fleet of foot, but balanced. Uses every bit of his wide frame. Coordinated with his hands to catch rushers.
cons: Carries hands oddly low at his sides in pass sets. Throws his timing off a lot. No hip drive in the run game. Leans on guys. Still a project yet turns 24 in June.
where_wins: NA
what_role: NA
what_improve: NA
bottom_line: Eze is well behind the learning curve for a player his age. He's a project without project-esque testing numbers.

blurb: Faalele had never played American football before traveling from Australia to IMG Academy in Florida back in 2016. The mammoth of a man immediately drew interest from college coaches across the country but settled on Minnesota after P.J. Fleck flew his mother out for a recruiting visit. Still new to the game, Faalele's ascent has been slow and steady after starting since his true freshman year. He returned after opting out in 2020 to have easily his highest-graded year. The allure of what his size and movement skills can end up doing in the NFL will be strong. Bradenton, FL
pros: One of the largest players in college football history at 6-foot-9, 380 pounds. Impervious anchor. He just doesn't get moved backwards. Only been playing football for five years and has improved considerably every year.
cons: Does he have the killer instinct? Not much iolence to his game. Limited dropback pass protection reps by design in Minnesota offense. Hands like Ricky Bobby — unsure what to do with them too often.
where_wins: SIZ E He wins with immovability at the moment. With good enough mirror ability, Faalele presents a massive road block who defenders have to go around.
what_role: P R OJECT T A CKLE You aren't drafting Faalele with 2022 in mind. Similar to another Aussie in Jordan Mailata, Faalele is a three- or four-year vesting option for whoever drafts him
what_improve: MEN T A LIT Y Hand placement, pass sets, mentality — you name it, he can probably improve there. He's still playing good football without being close to a finished product.
bottom_line: Faalele has unparalleled physical tools in addition to the kind of upward career progression teams can buy into.

blurb: Fortner went from rotational guard in to starting guard in 2019 and 2020 to finally starting center as a sixth-year senior in 2021. It was the center position that really tapped into his high-level football IQ and you saw him flourish from a grading perspective. While he has the body type and experience 3-4 at all three interior positions, it's that processing speed that sets him apart at center. He cleared out pockets for quarterback Will Levis regularly this past fall. Sylvania, OH
pros: Will-imposing upper body strength. Sends rushers off their path. Eyes work so quickly. Was a menace vs. Georgia's stunts last fall. Rodeo cowboy hanging on blocks. He's not letting go.
cons: Not a space player. Limited when locating linebackers. Real issues getting off double teams. Doesn't have the foot speed to react. Grade didn't reach high-level until late in career and turns 24 in May.
where_wins: NA
what_role: NA
what_improve: NA
bottom_line: Fortner brings a steady, powerful presence to the middle of your offense with all three interior position versatility.

blurb: Green came into the 2021 season as a potential top tackle, and it was his versatility that ended up hurting his draft stock. He was a starting right guard in 2019 as a true freshman and left guard in 2020. This past fall, he was supposed to be their starting right tackle, but after injuries struck, he started at four different line positions the first six weeks of the season. His tape at left guard for the final four games of last season should give you a good idea of what he's capable of. Humble, TX
pros: Flexibility and strength in his lower half is top notch. Extremely versatile. Played every position except center in 2021. Gets on linebackers so quickly at the second- level that it catches them off guard.
cons: Bear-hugger. Approaches blocks with exceedingly wide hands. Ducks into blocks on the move instead of gathering his lower half. Penalty issues at start of 2021. Seven penalties in first eight games.
where_wins: EX P LOSIV EN ESS Green is the most explosive interior lineman in the class. His pop on contact is special, and he can absorb a hit as well. His performance and versatility as a true junior is why he's so coveted.
what_role: V ER SA T ILE OL Green is still early enough along in his development that someone could easily make him a tackle. His body type enables you to slot him into any position along the offensive line.
what_improve: H A N D U SA G E Hand usage is the biggest room for growth. Obviously, that will improve with more consistent reps at one position, but he still needs to carry them tighter to his frame.
bottom_line: Once Green stopped getting jostled around and could focus on playing solely left guard, his tape was elite.

blurb: Goedeke redshirted in 2018 before taking over as the starting right tackle in 2019. He showed out in his very first season with an 81.4 overall grade on 1,031 snaps before tearing his ACL and missing all of 2020. In 2021, he not only returned to form, but looked like a new man altogether. He took his consistency to another level. On 321 run blocking snaps, Goedeke was downgraded all of 17 times all season. He'll be a guard convert, but a damn good one. Whitelaw, WI
pros: Outstanding and consistent hand placement. Quick to establish leverage and reset. Eyes work in unison with his feet. Quick to recognize stunts. Uncoils hips into contact. Can deliver and absorb blows.
cons: Length issues on the edge. Defenders lived in pads. Will have to kick inside. Took advantage of middling competition. Grades weren't same when faced better schools. Missed all of the 2020 season with an ACL tear.
where_wins: CON SIST EN CY Goedeke already looks like an NFL offensive linemen with his snap-to-snap technique. He's not the most physically imposing, but won't be out of place in the league.
what_role: GUARD His arm length would be an issue in the league if kept at tackle. That won't be nearly as much of the case at guard where his hand usage can shine.
what_improve: H EA LT H With no massive glaring technical weaknesses, Goedeke's main concerns are physical in nature. After an ACL tear and now hamstring, he just needs to stay on the field.
bottom_line: Goedeke is a plug-and-play guard that profiles to an above-average starter in time.

blurb: Hayes broke into the starting lineup as a redshirt sophomore at left guard back in 2019 and hasn't given up the job. That first season he actually performed admirably and didn't allow a single sack or hit in pass protection. That's been his calling card the last three seasons, as his run blocking finally started to catch up in 2021. It's worth wondering if he'll ever be a plus player in that regard at the next level, though, given his physical tools. Maryland Heights, MO
pros: Continually works upward into contact as a run-blocker. Very good at gaining leverage. Long arms for a guard and plus-latching ability. particularly explosive player. Some of the best independent hand usage in the class.
cons: Slowly narrows his base and gets more upright in pass sets as the play develops. Lethargic out of his stance. Just not a Nine penalties in 2021.
where_wins: H A N D U SA G E Hayes wins with elite hand usage. He has great length for a guard and is able to keep flailing defensive tackles at bay one-on-one.
what_role: GUARD Hayes is a guard-only due to his athletic profile, and he's probably not who you want running outside zone or pulling a ton. His best work is in a phonebooth.
what_improve: P LA Y IN G LOW Hayes has to sink lower in his pass sets or he'll get walked back into NFL pockets consistently. The good thing is that he's proven capable of doing so in the run game.
bottom_line: Hayes isn't particularly versatile, but he's not too far off from being a plus pass-protecting guard at the next level.

blurb: There was a time where it looked like Ingram might be the next big thing. He earned a 72.3 overall grade as a true freshman in 2017. However, he missed all of 2018 after he was charged with two counts of aggravated sexual assault of a minor. Those charges were eventually dropped, and Ingram was reinstated in 2019. He wasn't handed his starting job back and struggled as a rotational player at left guard during LSU's championship season. He's been a full-time starter every since, but he's never quite been able to build upon that promise he showed early on. DeSoto, TX
pros: Well proportioned guard that can get out and move. People mover. Packs a punch in the run game despite below average weight for guard. Starting experience at both guard positions with 2,682 career snaps to his name.
cons: Struggles to engage consistently. Hands are nothing special Feet and hands on different pages too often. Will go into contact with shaky footing. Stalled career progression. Never graded out particularly well.
where_wins: P OP ON CON T A CT Ingram wins by ending pass-rushing reps before they start. His first punch can deaden the most adept of rushers. He's got tailor-made guard traits.
what_role: GUARD He's a guard an preferrably in a power/counter heavy scheme. He's at his best when pulling around the edge.
what_improve: H A N DS Ingram has no problem delivering a blow, but his inability to maintain after first contact is why his grade is so lackluster. It will only get more difficult to do so in the NFL.
bottom_line: He'll be a starting guard in the league, but his lack of development throughout his career is concerning.

blurb: Johnson spent two years at Davidson before the last three at Boston College. Even after five years of college, Johnson turned only 22 last November. He's seen a very linear progression to his grading profile for the Eagles despite spending the season at left tackle. This past season, he 1-2 looked like the closest thing to a plug-and- play NFL guard. There are very few ugly losses or bad games on his tape to scare you off. Upper Marlboro, MD
pros: Lab-built guard frame. Loaded up lower half. picking up stunts/blitzes. Pad level is tremendous. Absorbs contact and delivers blows at an NFL-level. Purposeful in his movements. Everything works in unison.
cons: Most downgrades are awareness related when Average get-off and quickness for a guard. Bit of a late bloomer, grading didn't take off until Year 5.
where_wins: CON SIST EN CY He wins with all-around consistency. Johnson recorded one of the lowest downgrade rates among offensive linemen in college football this season. He doesn't allow himself to be put in bad positions.
what_role: ST A R T IN G G U A R D Johnson is a Day 1 starting guard.
what_improve: N OT MU CH Johnson's appeal is that his con section is darn near blank. He's obviously not perfect by any means, but he doesn't have glaring weaknesses on tape.
bottom_line: Johnson is an all-around pro-ready guard who's one of the safer bets in the draft class.

blurb: Coming out of Salt Lake City, Jones couldn't even land an offer from his hometown Utes. After landing at Southern Utah, Jones didn't really breakout until his third year with the Thunderbirds. While we only have this past fall fully graded, he was still tremendous in pass protection in the two years prior. 2021, however, was special as he earned single game grades of 80.0+ for seven straight games in the middle of the season.His Senior Bowl performance really solidified that he's not a fluke as he earned a 92.4 run blocking grade in the game. Murray, UT
pros: Massive upper body. Broad shoulders and long arms to envelope defenders. Great depth out of his stance in pass pro. No issues matching speed. Not going to let you go once he's got you. Does well to get into pads and stay there.
cons: Tendency to get high in his pass sets and unable to gain leverage. Late hands and slow to reset. Got by clamping shoulders of lesser competition. Odd frame with very thin lower half and massive upper body.
where_wins: U P P ER BODY ST R EN G T H It's not uncommon to see a scoop block end with Jones throwing someone to the turf. He has the kind of power behind his hands that every tackle wants.
what_role: DEV ELOP MEN T A L T A CKLE He's not a complete rebuild project, but Jones isn't a day one starter either. He'll be a starter at some point on his rookie deal.
what_improve: T IMIN G It's not uncommon for long-armed tackles to struggle to consistently time them up and Jones is no exception. He has little more in his repetoire than catching opposing edge rushers.
bottom_line: Jones may not have faced top competition, but he's closer to contributing than you might expect given that.

blurb: Jurgens redshirted as a freshman before breaking into the starting lineup at center in 2019. He's remained in the starting lineup there ever since. It wasn't always pretty with Jurgens who had massive issues with his location ability early on in his career. While that's still a worry, we've already seen him make massive strides in that regard. If he continues that upward trajectory in the NFL, his ceiling can push as high as anyone at the position n the draft class. Beatrice, NE
pros: Lightning off the snap. Any direction he wants to go, he gets there in a hurry. Can go toe-to-toe with a head-up nose despite barely tipping scales at 300 pounds. Gets so low into contact and on the move. One heck of an athlete.
cons: Plays at a frenetic pace. Leads to a lot of whiffs. Delivers blow more so than engaging. Won't bring his hands with him into contact. Eyes get stuck at the line of scrimmage on combos and is late to react to linebackers.
where_wins: LOWER BODY EX P LOSIV EN ESS When Jurgens uncoils his hips he puts some awe-inspiring reps on tape. He can really take guys for rides when he catches them.
what_role: CEN T ER I guess he could play elsewhere in a pinch, but with 2,066 snaps in his career at center why mess with a good thing? He can also operate in any scheme in the NFL.
what_improve: P LA Y IN G U N DER CON T R OL Watching Jurgens' tape can make one anxious. He plays in such a rush to get to his assignment that your own heart rate can't help but speed up watching.
bottom_line: Jurgens has all-pro type of physical ability but just needs more seasoning.

blurb: No one in college football has a stronger run-blocking track record over the past three seasons. Since taking over at right tackle in 2019, Kinnard has earned 90.0-plus run-blocking grades every single year. The worries come in pass protection. Kentucky was one of the run-heaviest Power Five teams in America during his first two years as a starter until Liam Cohen came over from the Rams and installed more pro-style concepts in 2021. While Kinnard made serious strides in pass pro last season, he's still a big work in progress in that regard. Cleveland, OH
pros: Stone-cold killer mentality. Will pancake defenders then dive on top. The torque he can generate is insane. He throws around 300-pounders. Thick build. Holds 345 pounds with ease. because he's the biggest dude on the field.
cons: Pass set technique is non-existent and need to be rebuilt from the ground up. Heavy on his feet and struggles mightily resetting them to recover. Late and wide hands. Gets by with bear hugging
where_wins: P H Y SICA LIT Y Kinnard wins by being the baddest man on the block. He was bigger and stronger than every player he had to block on a college field. That won't always be the case in the NFL, but he's still going to be a people mover.
what_role: GUARD Kinnard is a guard. Unless you want him to completely remake his body, that's where he ends up in the NFL. He also profiles as one who may need some seasoning as a backup.
what_improve: H A N D U SA G E While his pass sets need a complete overhaul, they're also indicative of his larger hand usage issues. He can't get by on pure physicality at the next level.
bottom_line: While he has intriguing play strength and power to work with, Kinnard's technique has a long way to go before he can see the field.

blurb: Kramer is just your run o fthe mill five-year starter who's never taken a snap at anything other than center. Kramer was part of Lovie Smith's first recruiting class with the Illini and one of his most prolific players. He's a high-end athlete for the position, but doesn't possess the requisite physicality to fit into most schemes in the league. You saw that even in his grading profile at the collegiate level. Hinsdale, IL
pros: Above-average get-off. Wins by getting on you in a hurry. Can fly between assignments. Foot quicks and processing speed to clean up stunts/slants. Natural leverage at his size. If he catches DTs off balance he can run with them.
cons: Not much to his lower half and won't fully unlock hips into contact. Looks ready to topple over at any moment on the move. Sixth-year player. Turns 24 in June.
where_wins: NA
what_role: NA
what_improve: NA
bottom_line: Kramer is a physically limited center who won't register on the radar of teams that aren't outside zone heavy.

blurb: There hasn't been a better college center since we started grading in 2014. He came in as a defensive lineman before redshirting and switching to the offensive side of the ball. Even though he was still extremely undersized and looked like an H-back, Linderbaum locked down the starting center position in 2019 and hasn't looked back. That year he earned an 81.7 overall grade before becoming the highest- Bigger graded center in college football each of Jason the past two seasons. Kelce Solon, IA
pros: The most athletic offensive lineman in college football. Flies around the field. Wrestling background that's apparent due to how strong his hands are on tape. Made massive strides in play strength over career. Legitimate people mover.
cons: Two-hand puncher. Needs to use hands more independently when deciphering stunts/slants. Center only at his size. Played in a perfect scheme to highlight his strengths. Can't bank on that in the NFL.
where_wins: A T H LET ICISM How much time you got? Linderbaum wins with freaky athleticism for a center. Guys that move like him usually dominate at 3-technique and not offensive line. His hands, balance, play strength and processing are also top notch.
what_role: Z ON E CEN T ER While he's talented enough to play guard in a pinch, don't move him from center. A scheme that gets its linemen on the move would be best suited for his skillset.
what_improve: IN DEP EN DEN T H A N DS His hand placement in pass protection is about the only red flag on an otherworldly resume. Because of how impressive his hands are in the run game, Linderbaum should easily be able to improve in that regard.
bottom_line: Linderbaum is the best center prospect we've seen at PFF since we started grading college in 2014.

blurb: Lindstrom showed up to Boston College in 2017 at 230 pounds before taking a redshirt year. He got up to 280 pounds by his redshirt freshman season in 2018 before cracking the starting lineup at 290 pounds in 2019. He's been starting at center ever since but has seen his weight plateau over that span. He's been tremendous in pass protection with only 24 pressures allowed on 1,181 career pass-blocking snaps. Dudley, MA
pros: Bounces around in pass protection with ease. Not going to be beaten by quicks alone. Assignment sure with plus awareness. A true field general at the position. Three years of starting experience and 2,574 snaps to his name.
cons: Undersized with limited length. Unlikely to put on much more mass as he turns 24 in July. Struggles passing off/picking up stunts. Doesn't have the pop to deaden. Protected in BC's scheme. Didn't fare nearly as well on an island at the Shrine Bowl.
where_wins: A G ILIT Y Lindstrom has some of the best mirror ability at the position in the class. He can quickly navigate to provide help elsewhere when left uncovered in pass protection.
what_role: CEN T ER ON LY Lindstrom will have to stay at center and likely go to a scheme that doesn't leave him on an island.
what_improve: MA SS Lindstrom has to get bigger. He has to get stronger. There's no sugar coating it.
bottom_line: Lindstrom will have an uphill climb to a roster spot given his lack of size and versatility.

blurb: Lucas may get a bad rep as an "air raid tackle," but that is a disservice to what he's done throughout his career at Washington State. On 2,195 career pass-blocking snaps across four years as a starter, Lucas has allowed a total of 49 pressures — that's it. His technique will need to improve, but the fact that he's gotten by so well with unrefined hand usage is almost a plus at this point. Everett, WA
pros: Battle tested in pass protection with 2,195 career snaps as a pass-blocker. Ideal tackle frame with the size and length of an NFL tackle. Light on his feet for his size. Mirroring ability is starting caliber in the NFL.
cons: Wide hands in pass protection leave pads open. He'll get bull rushed to death in NFL. Little experience in the run game and what he did wasn't particularly translatable. Powerful frame but doesn't play a particularly powerful game.
where_wins: MIR R OR Lucas wins by being able to move his massive 320-pound frame in an athletic manner. With the space created in Washington State's offense, Lucas didn't need much more than positioning.
what_role: T A CKLE Lucas is a tackle at the NFL level, but he's also a project despite his experience.
what_improve: T ECH N IQU E A lot. Washington State's scheme and development did him no favors when projecting to the NFL. A good portion of his game will need reworked.
bottom_line: Lucas has the physical traits of a starting tackle in the NFL, but he won't start right away.

blurb: Mitchell was the highest-graded tackle in the country last season, but that was no surprise after steadily seeing his grade climb in all four years as a starter. He split time early in his career between left and right tackle before ultimately residing on the right side the past two seasons. The competition level is a concern with him, but he allowed only one pressure on 47 pass-blocking snaps in his lone Power Five game last year against Texas. Monroe, LA
pros: Gorgeous pass sets. Impressive depth and balance Plays such an under-control brand of football. Won't see this guy on the ground. Impressive body control and flexibility for a tackle. Consistently gains leverage.
cons: Listed under 300 pounds and will have problems at that weight in the NFL. Low competition level. Texas was only Power-5 team on his schedule in 2021. He can get flat-backed on contact even when technique is sound. Middling power.
where_wins: CON SIST EN CY Consistent technique. Mitchell's hand placement, footwork and patient play style are a joy to watch. Even though it's a big competition level change, he could start early.
what_role: T A CKLE- G U A R D Mitchell is likely to be tabbed by some as a tackle-to-guard convert, and I wouldn't blame guard-needy teams for doing so. With added strength to his frame, though, he can stick at tackle.
what_improve: SIZ E Size and physicality are the biggest things with Mitchell. He's not the kind of athlete that can get by barely scraping 300 pounds. He needs to pack on some pounds.
bottom_line: While Mitchell isn't going to blow anyone away physically, he's consistent and versatile.

blurb: Munford has seen time ever since his true freshman year in 2017 when he played 149 snaps at right tackle. The next season he locked down the starting left tackle role which he held for the next three years. Munford swallowed his pride and kicked inside this past fall. It wasn't because he lost his job, but rather because it gave Ohio State their best five offensive linemen on the field and he was better suited for guard than their other two tackles. That cross- training should only make him more appealing for NFL evaluators. Massillon, OH
pros: Versatile, thick frame. Long arms and wide base. Knows how to use length to advantage. Snatches instead of punching already. One of the most experienced OL in the draft. 3,142 career snaps across three positions.
cons: Waist-bender with balance issues that persist across positions. Foot quickness isn't ideal. Has to be protected s. speed. Leans into contact instead of exlpoding. Not much of a people mover despite size.
where_wins: LEN G T H 35+ inch arms are insanely long for an interior lineman and Munford wins a lot of reps with them. He's quick to lock out and hold defenders at a distance.
what_role: SWIN G T A CKLE/ G U A R D Munford isn't a high end athlete, but he has tackle traits and put up better tape at that position in 2020 than he did at guard last year.
what_improve: BA LA N CE At this point, I'm not sure Munford is ever going to completely fix his waist bending. It's just a part of his game that you'll have to live with in the NFL.
bottom_line: Munford is experienced enough and technical enough to see the field at tackle or guard. I'm just not sure you'll ever be excited about him at either.

blurb: Neal is next in the prodigious pedigree of true freshman starters under Nick Saban. He started at left guard his first season in before kicking to right tackle in 2020 and left tackle this past year. Despite flip-flopping every single year of his career, he still saw his overall grade take steps forward in each of Top-10 those seasons. That versatility for a player of his size is what NFL teams will covet. Bradenton, FL
pros: A true behemoth. Not going to outphysical him at 6-foot-7, 350 pounds. Explodes out of stance. Moves like a man 50 pounds lighter. Started at a different position every year of his career. Invaluable cross-training
cons: Weight consistently out over his toes as a run- and pass-blocker. On the ground after first contact far more than you'd like. Struggles with stunts and when reacting to unexpected post-snap movement.
where_wins: P H Y SICA LIT Y Pure, unadulterated physicality. He can do things when he gets his hands on defenders that are unfathomable for a true junior. The term "freak" gets overused, but he qualifies.
what_role: A LL- A R OU N D T A CKLE He's a starting NFL tackle, and his experience at both tackle spots means you won't have to necessarily worry about a Penei Sewell situation early on.
what_improve: BA LA N CE Neal's propensity to overextend himself and get top heavy is a massive concern. The good news is he's improved those areas from 2020, but they still aren't solved by any means.
bottom_line: What Neal has, can't be coached. He's a special physical talent who is only scratching the surface.

blurb: Parham first started at left guard as a redshirt freshman back in 2018. After another season at left guard in 2019, Parham moved to right tackle in 2020 and right guard this past season. However, it was that 2020 season that really put him on the map. Despite being on the shorter end for the position and listed at 285 pounds, Parham had dominant tape at times out on the edge. While his frame was always going to be better suited at guard or center in the NFL, the ability he showed to play in space helped his draft stock immensely. Carrollton, GA
pros: Dude can move. Heck of an athlete for an offensive lineman. Special flexibility. The depth he gets in his stance is a prime example. Feet never stop driving. Very quick to reset and replace.
cons: Such a thin frame for a guard. Unique body type for a lineman. Struggles absorbing contact when picking up stunts or trying to make a reach block. Miss. State was the only Power-5 school on his schedule over the past two seasons.
where_wins: QU ICK Parham just gets on defenders so quickly. He's not a brute who can overpower defenders, but you see him win the first strike and leverage battles consistently.
what_role: CEN T ER - G U A R D At his size right now, center would make the most sense for him even though he's never played there. It won't take much for him to be a starting guard, either.
what_improve: H EF T Parham's weight is obviously the biggest area for improvement. There aren't a lot of 285-pound offensive linemen in the NFL nowadays. That concern is only exacerbated by the competition he faced.
bottom_line: There's so much to like about Parham's tape, but his pre-draft process performance will be just as important to his overall draft position.

blurb: Paul started his career off at right guard back in 2018 before switching to left guard in 2019 . Then he kicked out to tackle where he earned the highest grade of his career back in 2020 before struggling there this past fall. A big reason for that was competition level. Paul got explosed by the likes of Ohio State and Houston on his schedule this past fall. He didn't alleviate any of those concerns at the Senior Bowl where he earned a 21.1 pass-blocking grade throughout the week of practices. Ultimately he's a guard in the NFL. Houston, TX
pros: Insanely built lower half. Some of the thickest legs in the class. Surprisingly quick for a man his size. No issues getting out in space. Power throughout entire frame. Upper body can deliver a blow as well.
cons: Balance in his sets is non-existent. Feet and hands disjointed. Lack of urgency in his game. A tick slow reacting in pretty much everything. Attack angles are a mess. In bad positions in both run and pass game regularly.
where_wins: R A W T OOLS You see insane reps on his tape that make you confused as to why he can't do that every time. There may not be a better pure athlete for the guard position in the draft class.
what_role: DEV ELOP MEN T A L G U A R D While he doesn't have physical limitations that prevent him from playing tackle, he's had such issues eliminating space that guard seems like a better fit. He's got top tier guard physical traits.
what_improve: OV ER SET T IN G This is more his entire pass sets, but "oversetting" is a good shorthand for his problems. He can't stay on balance in his sets and as such can't react to anything unexpected.
bottom_line: Paul the athlete is incredible. Paul the football player is a non-starter.

blurb: You absolutely will not see more dominant run-blocking tape at the Division 1 level than the one Penning produced last year for Northern Iowa. In all, 9 of his 12 outings earned run-blocking grades over 90.0 — It was child's play for the 6-foot-7, 325- pounder. It's not only that he possesses elite 1-2 physical tools but also that he possesses the kind of killer instinct to play to through the whistle snap after snap. Sometimes it gets him in trouble, as evidenced by his penalties in his last 31 games, but you'd rather have to tone it down than coach it Mason City, IA
pros: Tape at Northern Iowa looks like someone's dad subbed into a pop warner game. So damn wide. Some insanely broad shoulders even by large man standards. The kind of physicality that transcends competition level. He is out for blood.
cons: Still far from perfect in pass protection. Obvious level of competition concerns. Not tested at all. Location ability in space leaves a lot to be desired. Not going to be his game.
where_wins: P OWER Penning wins with a silly combination of power and flexibility. He can sink low for a 6-foot-7 tackle and forklift opposing defenders — a good combination that translates to the run game.
what_role: G A P - SCH EME T A CKLE Gap scheme teams, come get your man. You want this guy firing into defenders and setting the tone as much as possible. You could flip him to the right side, but he's a tackle.
what_improve: ST A Y IN G LOW Penning obviously needs reps against top competition. In pass protection, he has a tendency to play high, which will get him bull rushed to death in the league if that persists.
bottom_line: Penning has a unique profile and much of his success hinges on continued development. Worst-case scenario, he's still a quality run blocker.

blurb: Petit-Frere broke into Ohio State's starting lineup at right tackle as a redshirt sophomore in 2020 before flipping to start at left tackle this past season. Your opinion of his tape will vary greatly depending on which game you watch. And that's because 19 of his 26 pressures allowed last season came against Michigan (8), Penn State (6) and Nebraska (5). A couple of those schools just so happen to have NFL- caliber edge rushers. That's not a death knell to his draft stock, but it's concerning Tampa, FL
pros: Gets out of his stance so easily for a 315-pound tackle. Ideal tackle frame with a thick and powerful lower half. Experience starting at both tackle positions. losing his confidence during games.
cons: Base has a tendency to get wide in pass protection, which limits recoverability. Leaves his pads completely exposed. Hands don't do him any favors. Would let things go from bad to worse due to
where_wins: T R A IT S He wins by ticking a ton of boxes physically. His frame, length and play strength are all top notch. He can get on defenders quickly and with some juice. Those are all very good starting points.
what_role: V ER SA T ILE OL Petit-Frere's body type is versatile enough to fill any position on the offensive line. He could start at guard early on and grow into a tackle role as his technique improves.
what_improve: H A N D U SA G E Petit-Frere has to use his hands better. It's fixable, but that's also easier said than done. His timing and placement are both issues.
bottom_line: He was exposed on tape too frequently to covet high in the draft, but he still has starting-caliber physical ability.

blurb: Poe is one of the most well-traveled prospects in the draft class. He started at Hutchinson Community College before transferring to Lenoir-Rhyne in 2018. After two seasons there, his 2020 season got cancelled and Poe transferred to Mercer. There he put himself on the map with an impressive showing against Alabama in Week 2 this past fall. His high-end athletic traits show up on the move and it's got NFL Smaller teams thinking about converting the Shaq squatty-body to fullback as well. Mason Fitzgerald, GA
pros: One twitched up offensive lineman. Looks like an athlete in everything he does. Out for blood on the move. The best pulling guard in the class. Only allowed one pressure on 24 pass-blocking snaps vs. Alabama in 2021.
cons: Short and slight. Only position he profiles to realistically is center. Overly aggressive without the technical prowess to do so. Low-level of competition with fairly unimpressive grades.
where_wins: NA
what_role: NA
what_improve: NA
bottom_line: With his movement skills at this size, there's a lot to work with from a developmental standpoint in the later rounds.

blurb: There isn't nearly enough space for a proper background of Raimann. He grew up in Austria, came to the USA as a foreign exchange student, and secured a scholarship at Central Michigan after one year of high school football. He started his career at tight end for two seasons before switching to tackle the past two seasons. He's put on 60 pounds over that span yet maintained his tight end athleticism. His progression in technique over that span, and even weekly, has been a sight to Delton, MI
pros: He can fly. One heck of an athlete for the position. He's only been playing OT for two years! Started his career at tight end. Slim but not weak. Play strength is fantastic for his size.
cons: Arm length is on the low end for the position, barely hitting 33-inch cutoff. Grade pumped up by low competition level; although, he did face LSU and Missouri. Has put on 60 pounds in two years but still could stand to pack on mass.
where_wins: H A N DS Raimann still moves around the football field like a tight end, but those hands that used to catch passes now catch defensive linemen. His hand placement in the run game is already outstanding.
what_role: LEF T T A CKLE Raimann is a Day 1 starting left tackle in the NFL. He may be new to the position, but I wouldn't classify him as a project.
what_improve: SIZ E He's nowhere near as physically dominant as others in the tackle class. He needs to continue to fill out his frame.
bottom_line: As crazy as it is to say for a guy who's played the position for two years, Raimann's tape is the most polished of any tackle in the draft.

blurb: Rhyan has been starting at left tackle for the Bruins ever since he showed up to campus. It didn't go so hot for him out the gate with 37 pressures allowed that first season, but he's seen marked improvement in the two years since. You could even see it from the first half of 2021 to the second where his grade lept from 75.9 to 86.4. That's the kind of trajectory you want to see heading into the league. Raw Braden San Juan Capistrano, CA
pros: Tremendous guard build. Massive lower half and insanely large hands. Unloads into contact. The kind of guy that can cave in his side of the line. Massive year-on-year progressions. Could even see it week-to-week in 2021.
cons: So overly aggressive. Comes off the ball like a defensive lineman at times. Footwork on baseblocks can get away from him. Will bring his feet together. Very old for a true junior. Will turn 24 as a rookie.
where_wins: N A T U R A L A T H LET ICISM You see the rugby background with Rhyan on tape with how comfortable he is as a mover for a massive man. He's got undersized lineman athleticism in a jumbo package.
what_role: G U A R D WIT H T A CKLE V ER A T ILIT Y He has the movement skills for tackle although not the length. It's worth starting him at tackle, but more than likely he's a guard who can play tackle in a pinch.
what_improve: LA N DMA R KS Rhyan has a bad habit of overshooting his target whether it's pass protection or in the run game.
bottom_line: Rhyan is still coming along technically and will have to kick into guard, but the improvements he's already made give you hope.

blurb: Salyer has played a role on the Georgia line ever since his freshman year. While he served as the utility man his first two seasons, playing snaps at every position along the offensive line, Salyer primarily lined up at left tackle the past two seasons. Still, he'd pick up the slack when needed elsewhere. That versatility will serve him well at the next level but will likely be coveted as a guard. Atlanta, GA
pros: Powerful upper body. His first strike will deaden pass-rushers in their tracks. Experience at every single position along the offensive line. His balance in pass protection massively improved from 2020 to 2021.
cons: Waist-bender. Cheats with his upper body to get pad level low. Plays high on the move. Very limited ability to react in space. Georgia's scheme protected him a ton in pass protection.
where_wins: P OWER Salyer is a power player who plays an attacking brand of football. He's a poster boy for Georgia's physical offense.
what_role: CEN T ER / G U A R D He's an interior lineman in the NFL despite spending most of his time at tackle. Playing at guard will help alleviate some of his issues locating in space at tackle.
what_improve: WA IST - BEN DIN G Salyer's waist-bending is going to be exposed even more in the NFL than it was in college. The scary thing is that it was already exposed a good deal in college.
bottom_line: Salyer will look better at guard than he did at tackle for Georgia, but that won't be a cure all of his issues.

blurb: Shaffer was a backup his first two seasons with the Bulldogs. Then in only his second career start in 2019, Shaffer suffered a season ending neck injury. He returned as a stalward left guard in 2020 and 2021. This past season, though, was easily the worst of his career in terms of pass protection with 20 pressures allowed. Those issues came to a head towards the end of the year as he allowed 13 pressures in the SEC championship and playoffs combined. Ellenwood, GA
pros: Lots of sand in the pants. Kind of frame that projects very easily to guard in the NFL. Short set that can create large pockets. When he gets a first punch, it's over. Looked much improved in his technique at the Senior Bowl.
cons: Bear-hugger that relies on strength too much in pass protection Limited foot quickness. Not going to go find guys in space. Late bloomer. Turns 24 over the summer
where_wins: NA
what_role: NA
what_improve: NA
bottom_line: Shaffer is an experienced guard who profiles better in the run game than in pass pro. At his age, that may be all he is at this point

blurb: Smith came to Virginia Tech a tight end recruit before transitioning to the offensive line. It didn't take long for him to start seeing the field, though, as he made four spot starts at left guard as a redshirt freshman in 2018. He's been the full-time starter there the past three seasons. While Virginia Tech may not run the most diverse run concepts, Smith plays a well-rounded enough game to get by in most schemes. More Nimble Fitzgerald, GA
pros: Balance and fluidity that you don't often see on the interior. Sends shivers with his punch. NFL-caliber violence in pass pro. Finds linebackers better than his testing numbers would suggest.
cons: Length below where you'd like it for the guard position. Could stand to sustain blocks longer. Zero big- time blocks in the run game last year. Never took a next step from a grading perspective. Middling production.
where_wins: NA
what_role: NA
what_improve: NA
bottom_line: Smith's age and arm length are strong knocks against what was impressive pass protecting tape.

blurb: You could tell Smith was something special ever since his true freshman season in 2019. On only 108 run blocking snaps that year, he had four big-time blocks. If you extrapolate that to a full season it would have been top-10 in college football. We've seen marked improvement every year to him now leading all of college football in 2021 with 21 big-time blocks. Even still, he's about as blank a canvas as you can get from a technique standpoint. That blank canvas only turned 21 earlier in April and put up an absurd 92.3 overall grade last Fort Worth, TX
pros: Special power for a man his age. People moving capability others can only dream of. So flexible for a 324 pounder. In awe of the body positions he can play in. Some of the best hand strength you'll see from a prospect in this class.
cons: Carries hands low and by his side in pass pro. Need to be reworked.. No snap to snap consistency. Out there freestyling most plays. Going to get demolished with holding penalties in the NFL. 13 last season.
where_wins: BU LLY BA LL Smith is the big kid on the playground who grabs you by your shirt collar and what let go no matter how hard you smack him. He latches on and won't let go no matter what.
what_role: LEF T T A CKLE With 1,779 snaps to his name at left tackle, there's no use changing his position. He's borderline developmental, but you want this guy seeing the field ASAP.
what_improve: T ECH N IQU E This relates to pretty much any and every part of playing the position. There's not much "NFL- readiness" to what he does on tape from a technical standpoint.
bottom_line: Physically, Smith is on par with the top-tier of tackles in this class. He's raw as can be, but at his age he has time to get there.

blurb: Strange came to Chattanooga a 255- pound defensive end in 2016. It was a long uphill climb just to crack the 300 pound barrier which he only did in 2020. Still, his tape against the Power-5 competition over the years has consistently been impressive. This past fall against Kentucky he made a statement with a 78.8 overall grade and only one pressure allowed on 38 pass- blocking reps. While he didn't grade out exceptionally well at the Senior Bowl playing a brand new position in center, you once again saw the high-end traits from Knoxville, TN
pros: High-end explosiveness out of his stance. Gets on defenders so quickly. Perfect fit in an outside zone scheme. Some insane cutoffs/reaches on tape. Plays the position with an uncoachable edge. Loves to somersault defenders.
cons: Very lean lower half. Not quite the heft you want to absorb a blow. Wide base and forward lean in pass pro limits recover ability in pass pro. One game against FBS competition the last two years (Kentucky, 2021). Turns 24 as rookie.
where_wins: G ET OF F This one is usually reserved for defensive linemen, but Strange's first step flips the script. He's not the biggest guard on tape, but he still moves people by being able to win leverage battles right at the snap.
what_role: Z ON E CEN T ER I don't think he should be particularly pigeonholed despite his skinnier frame, but there is no denying this is where he profiles best in the league. Any role that lets him fly off the ball is one I'm here for.
what_improve: P A SS SET S Between his wide base, wide hands, and forward lean - there's a number of things that need to be addressed to get his game NFL-ready. None seem too massive of a fix to worry long term.
bottom_line: There's so much to like about Strange's tape with many of his issues being fixable in time.

blurb: Tom started out as a center for the Demon Deacons where he first earned a starting role as a redshirt sophomore in 2019. He only kicked over to left tackle in where he immediately showed out as a pass protector. He only allowed 12 pressures on 370 pass-blocking snaps that year before taking his game to another level this past fall. Tom only allowed one pressure a game in one of the pass-happiest offenses in More Athletic America. He was especially impressive on Kelvin his 243 true pass sets earning an 88.4 grade. Beachum Baton Rouge, LA
pros: Independent hand usage is a big plus. Throws a lot at defenders. Easy, easy mirror ability. Tremendous feet in pass pro. Grip strength is a plus. Hands that can control defenders.
cons: Regularly walked back into the pocket. Thin lower half that needs to get stronger. More receiver than deliverer in the run game. Position blocker. Leaves pads exposed far too often.
where_wins: MIR R OR Tom take short choppy steps keeping him on balance and ready to react to whatever is thrown at him. He's almost never caught too far out of position.
what_role: T A CKLE WIT H V ER SA T ILIT Y There's obviously a push for him to play inside based on where he lined up at the Shrine Bowl, but there's nothing in his physical profile that says he can't stay at tackle.
what_improve: A N CH OR With his patient play style, Tom has to improve his lower body and core strength to hold up to the power he'll face in the NFL. He's not too far off, though.
bottom_line: Tom's mirror and hand usage is a great starting point for the tackle position in the NFL. He's a future starter.

blurb: It took Volson until his fourth season for the Bison in 2019 to lock down a starting role at right tackle. He's been primarily there ever since, but has actually taken snaps at all five offensive line positions. While he's been a tackle, he likely profiles to a guard at the NFL level with his athletic limitations and that's where he primarily lined up over the week of practices at the Shrine Bowl. Anamoose, ND
pros: Hands do a ton of work for him in pass pro. Strong and active. Extensive experience at both tackle and guard with the frame to play either. Showed out at the Shrine Bowl with the highest pass-blocking grade in the practices
cons: High-cut guard that cedes ground on contact. Difficult to win leverage battles. Lacks agility to be particularly versatile. Really see it on lackluster stunt work. Older prospect that turns 24 before the season.
where_wins: NA
what_role: NA
what_improve: NA
bottom_line: While he's not the project small school guys usually get branded as, Volson has middling physicality to project to the next level.

blurb: Waletzko has been starting for North Dakota ever since he arrived in 2018. He's missed time over the years with a knee injury in 2019 and a shoulder injury this past fall, but never played anywhere but left tackle the last three seasons. The outside is where he profiles best in the NFL. He's a long and agile tackle with the kind of tools that are tailor-made to pass protect in the NFL. He'll also be a weapon in the screen game where he can track down even defensive Cold Spring, MN
pros: Exceptionally broad human being. Measured an 86" wingspan at his pro day. So dang light on his for having a top-heavy build. Can really move in space. Shows the kind of sink and flexibility that's uncommon for a taller tackle.
cons: Mass all comes in his upper half. Oddly skinny legs for a tackle. Footwork and angles in pass sets are often non- existent. Little feel for the pocket. Grading was nothing special at low-level competition with few NFL pass pro concepts
where_wins: NA
what_role: NA
what_improve: NA
bottom_line: Waletzko ticks so many physical boxes of a high-end starting tackle, but his tape screams developmental project.

blurb: A former top-100 recruit, Walker took one redshirt year before he was tabbed as the starting left tackle for the next three years. For his first year as a starter, his 2019 season put him on draft radars as he earned a 69.7 overall grade. He made some strides in pass protection in 2020 season, but not nearly enough for him to declare that early. With high expectations in 2021, Walker fell drastically short from Week 1 where he earned a 49.0 overall grade against Wisconsin and onward with a meniscus tear causing him to miss the end of the season. Waldorf, MD
pros: Well proportioned tackle frame that immediately looks the part. Strong and flexible lower half that can sit down vs. bull-rushes. Feet churn in the run game. Never stop trying to displace defenders when engaged.
cons: Base widens and tightens willy-nilly in his pass sets. Feet do him no favors. Got stunted to death. Too heavy on heels in sets to react. Injuries torpedoed him in 2021. Tape was better the year prior.
where_wins: T A CKLE T R A IT S So few players on this earth move like NFL tackles and Walker is one of them. Being able to move and look athletic at his size is why he's going to get every chance to succeed at the next level.
what_role: SWIN G T A CKLE Walker has played enough ball and still not improved to the point where one might have to accept this is who he is. That's an NFL tackle, but it's likely a backup.
what_improve: BA LA N CE IN SET S Walker is too athletic to put some of the reps he did on tape. He gets himself in bad positions out of lack of attention to detail and loses balance.
bottom_line: Walker looks like an NFL tackle, but between lackluster tape and opting out of athletic testing, Walker's stock is going the wrong way.

blurb: You will not find many more experienced linemen in the history of college football. N/A After redshirting in 2016, Wattenberg went on to be a starter for five years with the Huskies! He's got starting experience at left N/A tackle, left guard, and center. The problem is, none of those seasons finished with 7-UDFA particularly impressive grades. His peak was this past season at a middling 72.7 overall. While that experience might be coveted, Longer that performance will not. Jimmy San Juan Capistrano, CA
pros: Plus ability to climb to the second-level and locate. Tight hands in the run game. Gaining initial engage is rarely his problem. 3,307 career snaps to his name across left tackle, left guard, and center.
cons: Nothing to his lower half. Walked back far too easily. Knocked off balance with any sort of jolt from a defender. No improvement from a grading perspective over the course of his career.
where_wins: NA
what_role: NA
what_improve: NA
bottom_line: Wattenberg looks the part until he has to impose his will. His play strength isn't at the level you want to start in the league.

blurb: West walked onto Arizona State's campus and was the starting center for his very first collegiate game. He switched to right guard midseason, left guard in 2020 and then finally landed back at center this past fall. All the while playing football well beyond his years. His grade would have taken a good leap forward each of those seasons were it not for him getting downgraded for an off-target snap seemingly ever other game. He's young and versatile - that's a good combo. Mission Hills, CA
pros: Smooth mover who plays a very under control brand of football. Won't turn 21 until May. Youngest IOL prospect in class. Consistent hand placement beyond his years. Low and inside to gain leverage.
cons: Below 300 pounds at combine. Upper body/core strength not quite at an NFL-level yet. Consistent issues with snap accuracy. A ton of botched snaps. Noticeable hitch out of his snap. More pronounced when moving to his left post-snap.
where_wins: BA LA N CE About the only time you see this guy on the ground is when he trips over someone else’s foot. West is such a natural athlete which is why he graded out so well early in his college career.
what_role: CEN T ER / G U A R D P R OJECT He's played 260+ snaps at all three interior line positions. He's likely a center at his size now but has room to grow into guard with a couple years in an NFL weight room.
what_improve: U P P ER BODY ST R EN G T H West's ability to maintain control of blocks suffers because of this. At his age, though, this is something one can certainly expect to improve.
bottom_line: West may take a while to get there physically, but it's all there to be a starting interior linemen in time.

blurb: A former top recruit, Booker has seen significant time ever since his true freshman year in 2018 and been a starter ever since 2019. Unfortunately, he never quite lived up to that lofty recruiting status as Bookers best year came as a sophomore. That year he posted his career high for sacks (6) and stops (32) despite playing 262 snaps fewer than this past fall. He's got athletic tools to work with and versatility that will be More Raw coveted. Dereke Baltimore, MD
pros: quicks are tremendous for a 300+ pounder. the Stanford defensive line. every alignment on the interior.
cons: A nightmare to handle on slants. First step game. Thick lower half that stands out immediately on When he does, they are late in snap. Versatile body type that can and has filled taken out of his gap entirely.
where_wins: EX P LOSIV E LOWER H A LF When everything fires in unison, Booker can put some awe inspiring reps on tape. He can fire off and turn the corner with the best of them.
what_role: V ER SA T ILE R OT A T ION A L DT This is pretty much what Booker has already been at Stanford. He doesn't look particularly out of place wherever he lines up.
what_improve: A WA R EN ESS Booker could easily develop into a starter once the game slows down for him. It's concerning that hasn't happened in four years at Stanford, though. Having a more well-defined role could help him out in this regard a lot.
bottom_line: Booker has high-end starter flashes and athleticism. They just come once in a blue moon.

blurb: Butler was a bit of a late bloomer in his five seasons with the Volunteers. It took until his redshirt sophomore year to lock down a rotational role, his redshirt junior year to lock down a starting role, and his redshirt senior year before he started to really make an impact. While averaging 55.8 snaps per game, Butler still managed to grade out well above-average as both a run defender and pass-rusher last fall. He was a havoc Poor Man’s creating 3-technique in Tennessee's Marlon defense and often got deployed on post- Davidson snap slants to try to take advantage of his Garner, NC
pros: a pass-rusher. better against doubles than expected. hands first.
cons: Active hands and plus motor. Lot of late wins as a three-technique. Can pinball off OL and still make plays. Held up better when given carte blanch to attack. Stays low out of his stance and leads with his rookie.
where_wins: EF F OR T Butler puts everything he has into every single play. You won't find many lethargic get-offs or lackluster pass-rush attempts on his tape.
what_role: 3 - T ECH Butler may not ever profile as a high-end playmaker at the next level, but don't be surprised if he's in a starting lineup at some point. He can get off the ball and create havoc.

Bearcats fans are glad he did, though, as he was instrumental in their storybook run to the College Football Playoffs. Even in the Alabama game, Sanders showed up in a big way with pressures. The one thing Bearcats fans weren't glad about, however, was his Banogu penalties. Sanders drew a ridiculous 20 flags over the past two seasons, which were mostly offsides. Jacksonville, FL
